hand/diff-geometry.html:
Second Fundamental Form and the Shape Operator

The first fundamental form encodes intrinsic metric data on a surface, but the way a surface sits in the ambient Euclidean space is captured by the second fundamental form. Given a regular parametrisation X(u,v) with unit normal N, the coefficients are L = ⟨Xuu, N⟩, M = ⟨Xuv, N⟩, N = ⟨Xvv, N⟩. The quadratic form II = L du² + 2M du dv + N dv² measures the normal component of the acceleration of curves on the surface. The shape operator S = −dN is the linear map on the tangent plane defined by S(v) = −∇vN. In matrix form relative to the basis {Xu, Xv}, S = I⁻¹ II where I is the first fundamental form matrix. The eigenvalues of S are the principal curvatures κ₁, κ₂; their product is the Gaussian curvature K = det(S) and their mean is the mean curvature H = ½ trace(S). The sign of K determines local shape: K > 0 elliptic (both principal curvatures same sign), K < 0 hyperbolic (opposite signs), K = 0 parabolic (one zero). The second fundamental form also appears in the Gauss and Codazzi–Mainardi equations, which are the integrability conditions for a surface to exist in ℝ³ with prescribed I and II. These equations link intrinsic curvature (via the Riemann tensor of I) to extrinsic data, providing a bridge between the Theorema Egregium and the full classification of surfaces up to rigid motions.

In practical computations, one often diagonalises the shape operator by choosing lines of curvature coordinates, where the coordinate curves are tangent to principal directions. In such coordinates the second fundamental form becomes diagonal, simplifying the expression of the Gauss equation to K = −(1/√EG) [ (∂/∂u)( (√G/√E) Γ¹₂₂ ) + (∂/∂v)( (√E/√G) Γ²₁₁ ) ]. This form is useful for proving that a surface of constant positive curvature is locally isometric to a sphere, while constant negative curvature yields the hyperbolic plane. The shape operator also governs the evolution of surfaces under normal flows: the normal velocity of a surface moving by mean curvature flow is exactly H, and the linearisation of this flow involves the Jacobi operator Δ + |S|², where |S|² = κ₁² + κ₂². Understanding the spectral properties of this operator is central to analysing singularity formation in geometric flows.

Parallel Transport, Holonomy, and the Ambrose–Singer Theorem

Parallel transport provides a way to compare vectors at different points of a Riemannian manifold by moving them along a curve while keeping them covariantly constant. Given a piecewise smooth curve γ : [0,1] → M and a vector v₀ ∈ Tγ(0)M, the parallel transport equation ∇γ̇ V = 0 with initial condition V(0)=v₀ has a unique solution V(t). The map Pγ : Tγ(0)M → Tγ(1)M sending v₀ to V(1) is a linear isometry. If γ is a closed loop based at p, the holonomy group Holp(M) consists of all such linear maps obtained from loops at p. The restricted holonomy group Hol⁰p(M) uses only contractible loops. The Ambrose–Singer theorem states that the Lie algebra of Hol⁰p(M) is generated by the curvature endomorphisms R(X,Y) evaluated at points reachable from p by horizontal curves in the frame bundle. In concrete terms, the curvature tensor completely determines the infinitesimal holonomy, and integrating these infinitesimal rotations along loops yields the full holonomy group.

For a surface, the holonomy around a small geodesic triangle equals the integral of Gaussian curvature over the enclosed region, a direct manifestation of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem. In higher dimensions, holonomy groups classify special geometries: Berger's list shows that irreducible, non‑symmetric holonomy groups are limited to SO(n), U(n/2), SU(n/2), Sp(n/4), Sp(n/4)·Sp(1), G₂ (n=7) and Spin(7) (n=8). Manifolds with reduced holonomy admit parallel spinors and play a central role in string theory compactifications. The holonomy group also controls the existence of parallel tensor fields: a parallel p‑form exists iff the holonomy representation fixes a non‑zero element in ΛpTpM. This principle underlies the construction of calibrated geometries and special Lagrangian submanifolds.

Worked Example: Holonomy on the 2‑Sphere
Compute the holonomy angle for parallel transport of a tangent vector around a geodesic triangle on the unit sphere S² with vertices at the north pole N, a point A on the equator at longitude 0, and a point B on the equator at longitude π/2. The triangle edges are meridians from N to A and N to B, and the equatorial arc from A to B.
On S² the Gaussian curvature K = 1 everywhere. The area of the spherical triangle is one eighth of the sphere’s total area 4π, so Area = π/2. By the Gauss–Bonnet theorem for a geodesic triangle, the sum of interior angles = π + ∫ K dA = π + π/2 = 3π/2. Each angle at the equator is π/2, the angle at the north pole is π/2, confirming the area. Parallel transport around the triangle rotates a vector by the holonomy angle equal to the enclosed curvature integral, i.e. ∫ K dA = π/2. Hence the vector returns rotated by 90°.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for holonomy on a surface, first identify whether the loop bounds a region where Gaussian curvature is constant or easily integrable. Use the area–curvature relation (holonomy = ∫ K dA) rather than solving the parallel transport ODE directly. For higher‑dimensional manifolds, recall Berger’s classification: if the holonomy is a proper subgroup of SO(n), the manifold admits special geometric structures (Kähler, Calabi–Yau, hyper‑Kähler, G₂, Spin(7)). Mentioning the relevant subgroup often earns full credit.

Cartan's Structure Equations and Moving Frames

Élie Cartan’s method of moving frames replaces coordinate‑dependent calculations with an orthonormal coframe {θ¹,…,θⁿ} and connection 1‑forms ωⁱⱼ satisfying ωⁱⱼ = −ωʲⁱ. The first structure equation expresses the exterior derivative of the coframe: dθⁱ = −∑ⱼ ωⁱⱼ ∧ θʲ. The second structure equation gives the curvature 2‑forms: Ωⁱⱼ = dωⁱⱼ + ∑ₖ ωⁱₖ ∧ ωₖⱼ. In this language the Riemann curvature tensor components are Rⁱⱼₖₗ = Ωⁱⱼ( eₖ, eₗ ). The Bianchi identities become dΩⁱⱼ + ∑ₖ ( ωⁱₖ ∧ Ωₖⱼ + Ωⁱₖ ∧ ωₖⱼ ) = 0. The power of the moving frame method lies in its adaptability: one chooses a frame adapted to the geometry (e.g., principal curvature directions on a surface, or a null frame in Lorentzian geometry) which often diagonalises the connection forms and simplifies the curvature equations dramatically.

For a hypersurface in ℝⁿ⁺¹, the Gauss formula relates the ambient connection to the induced connection and the second fundamental form hⁱⱼ: ωⁱⱼ = ω̄ⁱⱼ + hⁱⱼ θⁿ⁺¹, where ω̄ⁱⱼ are the connection forms of the induced metric. The Codazzi equation becomes dhⁱⱼ + ∑ₖ ( hⁱₖ ωₖⱼ + hₖⱼ ωⁱₖ ) = 0, and the Gauss equation reads Ωⁱⱼ = Ω̄ⁱⱼ − hⁱₖ ∧ hₖⱼ. These are exactly the classical Gauss–Codazzi equations in a coordinate‑free form. Cartan’s equivalence method uses the structure equations to decide when two G‑structures are locally equivalent: one prolongs the coframe bundle until the structure group is reduced to the identity, obtaining a complete set of invariants. This technique underlies the classification of homogeneous spaces, the solution of the isometric embedding problem for analytic metrics (Cartan–Janet theorem), and the construction of invariant differential operators on manifolds with special holonomy.

Comparison Theorems: Rauch, Toponogov, and Bishop–Gromov

Comparison geometry relates the metric properties of a Riemannian manifold to those of a model space of constant curvature. The Rauch comparison theorem controls the growth of Jacobi fields along geodesics. If sectional curvatures satisfy K ≤ κ, then the norm of a Jacobi field J with J(0)=0, |J'(0)|=1 is bounded below by the corresponding Jacobi field in the space form of curvature κ; if K ≥ κ the inequality reverses. This yields concrete estimates for the differential of the exponential map and for the distance between nearby geodesics. Toponogov’s triangle comparison theorem states that for a manifold with K ≥ κ, any geodesic triangle is “fatter” than the comparison triangle in the κ‑space form: the angle at a vertex is at least the corresponding model angle. Conversely, K ≤ κ gives “thinner” triangles. These theorems are the backbone of global Riemannian geometry: they imply the Cartan–Hadamard theorem (simply connected, K ≤ 0 ⇒ universal cover diffeomorphic to ℝⁿ), the sphere theorem (pinched positive curvature ⇒ homeomorphic to sphere), and the Cheeger–Gromoll splitting theorem (non‑negative Ricci curvature and a line ⇒ product with ℝ).

The Bishop–Gromov volume comparison theorem bounds the volume of geodesic balls. If Ric ≥ (n−1)κ, then the function r ↦ Vol(B(p,r)) / Vκ(r) is non‑increasing, where Vκ(r) is the volume of a ball of radius r in the κ‑space form. This monotonicity yields the relative volume comparison Vol(B(p,R)) / Vol(B(p,r)) ≤ Vκ(R) / Vκ(r) for 0 < r < R. As a corollary, the asymptotic volume ratio AVR = limr→∞ Vol(B(p,r)) / rⁿ is well defined and independent of p. Manifolds with non‑negative Ricci curvature have AVR ≤ ωₙ (the Euclidean volume), with equality only for flat ℝⁿ. The Bishop–Gromov inequality also underpins the compactness theory for sequences of manifolds with uniform Ricci lower bounds (Gromov’s precompactness theorem) and the definition of Ricci limit spaces in metric measure geometry.

Geometric Flows Beyond Ricci Flow: Mean Curvature Flow and Applications

While Ricci flow evolves the metric of a manifold, mean curvature flow (MCF) evolves a submanifold by moving each point in the normal direction with speed equal to the mean curvature vector H. For a hypersurface Σₜ ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹, the evolution equation is ∂ₜ X = H ν, where ν is the unit normal. MCF is the gradient flow of the area functional, so area decreases monotonically: d/dt Area(Σₜ) = −∫ |H|² dμ ≤ 0. Singularities inevitably form in finite time for closed hypersurfaces (e.g., a sphere shrinks to a point). Huisken’s monotonicity formula introduces a backward heat kernel weight centred at a potential singularity, showing that the Gaussian density Θ = limt→T ∫ Σₜ Φ(x₀,T) dμ is non‑decreasing and classifies tangent flows at singularities as self‑shrinkers satisfying H = ⟨X, ν⟩/2. The classification of self‑shrinkers in low dimensions (planes, spheres, cylinders) drives the surgery program for MCF, analogous to Perelman’s Ricci flow surgery.

Applications of MCF extend beyond pure geometry. In image processing, the level‑set formulation of MCF provides a curvature‑driven denoising algorithm that preserves edges while smoothing noise. In materials science, grain boundary motion in polycrystals is modelled by anisotropic MCF where the surface tension depends on the crystallographic orientation. The flow also appears in general relativity: the Hawking mass of a 2‑sphere in a spacelike slice is monotone under inverse mean curvature flow (where speed is 1/H), a fact used by Huisken and Ilmanen to prove the Riemannian Penrose inequality. Recent work on MCF with surgery in higher codimension and on ancient solutions (eternal solutions existing for all negative times) connects to the classification of singularity models and to the study of minimal varieties via the min‑max method. Understanding the interplay between curvature pinching, entropy functionals, and topological constraints remains a vibrant research frontier.

  • Confusing the second fundamental form with the shape operator: they are related by the metric but have different index positions and transformation rules.
  • Assuming holonomy equals curvature at a point; holonomy is a global (or at least loop‑dependent) quantity, while curvature is pointwise.
  • Misapplying Cartan’s structure equations by forgetting the torsion‑free condition when the connection is not Levi‑Civita.
  • Using Rauch comparison with the wrong curvature bound direction: K ≤ κ gives lower bounds on Jacobi fields, K ≥ κ gives upper bounds.
  • Thinking mean curvature flow preserves volume; it strictly decreases area and can change enclosed volume unless a volume‑preserving variant is used.
  • Overlooking that the Bishop–Gromov ratio monotonicity requires a Ricci lower bound, not just a sectional curvature bound.
  • Neglecting the role of the Ambrose–Singer theorem in linking curvature to the Lie algebra of the holonomy group, which is essential for classifying special geometries.

Cyclicity and Unit Digit Patterns in Powers

The unit digit of any integer power follows a fixed cycle that depends only on the unit digit of the base. For digits 0, 1, 5, 6 the cycle length is 1 — the unit digit never changes. For 4 and 9 the cycle length is 2: 4 → 6 → 4 … and 9 → 1 → 9 … . For 2, 3, 7, 8 the cycle length is 4. The sequence for 2 is 2, 4, 8, 6; for 3 it is 3, 9, 7, 1; for 7 it is 7, 9, 3, 1; for 8 it is 8, 4, 2, 6. To find the unit digit of ab, reduce the exponent b modulo the cycle length (using 4 for the four‑digit cycles, 2 for 4 and 9, 1 for the others). If the remainder is 0, use the last element of the cycle.

This principle extends to the last two digits when the base ends with 2, 3, 7, 8, or any number coprime to 100. The cycle length for the last two digits divides 20 (Carmichael function λ(100)=20). For example, powers of 2 modulo 100 repeat every 20: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 28, 56, 12, 24, 48, 96, 92, 84, 68, 36, 72, 44, 88, 76, then 52, 04 … . In examinations, the unit‑digit cycle is sufficient for the vast majority of questions; the two‑digit cycle appears only in higher‑difficulty papers.

A common twist is to ask for the unit digit of a sum or product of large powers, such as (7123 + 8456) mod 10. Compute each unit digit separately using the cycles, then add and take mod 10. Another twist embeds the exponent in a factorial or a combinatorial expression; reduce the exponent modulo the cycle length before applying the cycle.

Alligation with Three or More Components

Alligation is traditionally taught for two ingredients, but many mixture problems involve three or more components. The core idea remains weighted average: the overall concentration (or price) equals the sum of (quantity × concentration) divided by total quantity. When three components A, B, C with concentrations cA, cB, cC are mixed to give a mean concentration m, the quantities qA, qB, qC satisfy qA(cA−m) + qB(cB−m) + qC(cC−m) = 0. This single linear equation has infinitely many solutions; an additional condition (such as a given ratio between two components, or a fixed total quantity) pins down a unique ratio.

A practical shortcut is successive alligation: first combine two components into an intermediate mixture, then alligate that intermediate with the third component. For example, to mix teas at ₹200, ₹250, and ₹300 per kg to obtain ₹240 per kg, first alligate ₹200 and ₹300 to get a mixture at ₹240. The differences are 300−240=60 and 240−200=40, giving ratio 60:40 = 3:2 for the ₹200 and ₹300 teas. This intermediate mixture (call it M) has price ₹240. Now alligate M (₹240) with the third tea ₹250 to keep the final price ₹240. The differences are 250−240=10 and 240−240=0, implying the third tea must be added in zero quantity — which tells us the target price cannot be achieved with all three unless the third tea’s price equals the target. In a solvable case, say target ₹245, the second alligation gives a non‑zero ratio.

When the problem states “mix in the ratio 2:3:5” and asks for the resulting concentration, simply compute the weighted average: (2cA+3cB+5cC)/(2+3+5). Conversely, if the final concentration and two of the three ratios are known, set up the weighted‑average equation and solve for the unknown ratio. This algebraic approach is faster than drawing multiple crosses and avoids sign errors.

Examiners also test replacement problems disguised as alligation: a vessel contains a mixture; a portion is removed and replaced by a pure component. The concentration after n replacements follows Cn = C0(1−r/V)n + Cpure[1−(1−r/V)n], where r is the replaced volume and V the total volume. Recognising this pattern saves time compared to iterative alligation.

Three‑Component Alligation
A merchant mixes three varieties of rice costing ₹30, ₹40, and ₹50 per kg. He sells the mixture at ₹44 per kg, making a profit of 10% on cost. In what ratio must he mix the three varieties?
First find the cost price of the mixture. Selling price = ₹44, profit = 10% → CP = 44 ÷ 1.10 = ₹40 per kg. Now we need quantities q₁, q₂, q₃ for prices 30, 40, 50 such that weighted average = 40. Equation: (30q₁ + 40q₂ + 50q₃) / (q₁+q₂+q₃) = 40 → 30q₁ + 40q₂ + 50q₃ = 40q₁ + 40q₂ + 40q₃ → 10q₃ = 10q₁ → q₁ = q₃. The second variety (₹40) can be any amount because its price equals the mean; it does not affect the average. Thus the ratio is q₁ : q₂ : q₃ = 1 : k : 1, where k is any non‑negative number. The simplest integer ratio is 1 : 0 : 1, but a typical answer expects a definite ratio; if the problem states “all three varieties are used”, choose k = 1 → 1 : 1 : 1. Check: (30+40+50)/3 = 40. Correct.
Exam‑Day Strategy for Multi‑Component Mixtures
When you see three or more components, write the weighted‑average equation immediately. Identify which component’s price equals the target mean — that component’s quantity is free. Use the remaining two components to form a simple two‑component alligation. This reduces the problem to a familiar cross diagram and eliminates algebraic errors.

Profit and Loss with Successive Discounts and Marked Price Variations

Successive discounts are not additive; a 20% discount followed by a 10% discount is equivalent to a single discount of 28% (1 − 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.28). The general formula for two successive discounts d₁% and d₂% is equivalent discount = d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100. For three discounts d₁, d₂, d₃, apply the formula iteratively: first combine d₁ and d₂, then combine the result with d₃. This is faster than computing the final selling price step by step when only the equivalent discount is asked.

Marked price (MP) variations often appear as “the shopkeeper marks up by x%, then gives a discount of y%, then offers an additional discount of z% on the reduced price”. The effective selling price = MP × (1 + x/100) × (1 − y/100) × (1 − z/100). Profit or loss percentage is then calculated on cost price (CP). A common trap: the problem states “profit of 20% on selling price” — here the base changes from CP to SP. Convert by using Profit% on SP = (Profit/SP)×100 = (Profit/CP)×100 × (CP/SP). Since SP = CP × (1 + Profit% on CP/100), the conversion factor is 1/(1 + Profit% on CP/100).

Another variation: “A dealer sells an article at a 15% discount on the marked price and still makes a 20% profit on cost. If the cost price rises by 10% and the marked price is increased by 5%, what discount should be offered to keep the same profit percentage?” Set up the original relation: SP = 0.85 MP = 1.20 CP. After changes, new CP' = 1.10 CP, new MP' = 1.05 MP. Desired SP' = 1.20 CP' = 1.20 × 1.10 CP = 1.32 CP. But SP' = (1 − d/100) MP' = (1 − d/100) × 1.05 MP. Substitute MP = SP/0.85 = 1.20 CP/0.85. Solve for d. This algebraic method is systematic and avoids guesswork.

When the problem involves “buy x get y free” or “cash discount on bulk purchase”, treat the free items as a discount on the effective quantity. For “buy 4 get 1 free”, the customer pays for 4 but receives 5; effective discount = 1/5 = 20%. Combine this with any other discount using the successive‑discount formula.

Compound Interest with Varying Rates and Installments

Standard compound interest assumes a constant annual rate. When the rate changes each year, the amount after n years is A = P × ∏i=1..n (1 + Ri/100). For example, ₹10,000 invested at 8% for the first year, 10% for the second, and 12% for the third yields A = 10000 × 1.08 × 1.10 × 1.12 = ₹13,305.60. The compound interest is A − P. This product form is essential; do not average the rates and apply a single rate — that gives a wrong answer because compounding is multiplicative, not additive.

Installment problems (loans repaid in equal annual instalments) are solved using the present value of an annuity. If a loan of amount L is repaid in n equal yearly instalments of X at rate R% per annum compounded annually, then L = X × [1 − (1 + R/100)−n] / (R/100). Rearranged, X = L × (R/100) / [1 − (1 + R/100)−n]. This formula assumes the first instalment is paid one year after the loan is taken. If the first instalment is paid immediately (annuity due), multiply the right‑hand side by (1 + R/100).

A frequent twist: “A sum of ₹20,000 is borrowed at 10% p.a. compound interest and repaid in three equal annual instalments. Find the instalment amount.” Use the formula with L=20000, R=10, n=3. (1+R/100)=1.1. (1.1)−3 = 1/1.331 ≈ 0.7513. Denominator = 1 − 0.7513 = 0.2487. X = 20000 × 0.10 / 0.2487 ≈ ₹8,042. Check: after first year, amount = 22000; pay 8042 → balance 13958. After second year, 13958×1.1=15353.8; pay 8042 → balance 7311.8. After third year, 7311.8×1.1=8043 ≈ instalment. The small rounding difference is acceptable.

When rates vary across years for an instalment loan, the present‑value formula does not apply directly. Instead, work backwards from the last instalment: let the last instalment be X. The amount due just before the last payment is X. One year earlier, the amount due was X/(1+Rn/100). Add the (n−1)th instalment, and continue backwards. This recursive method handles any rate sequence.

Relative Speed on Circular Tracks and Meeting Points

On a circular track of length L, two runners starting from the same point and moving in the same direction with speeds v₁ > v₂ meet every L/(v₁−v₂) time units. The number of distinct meeting points on the track equals the number of times the faster runner laps the slower before both return to the start simultaneously. If the speeds are in the ratio a:b (in simplest terms), the number of distinct meeting points is |a−b|. For opposite directions, relative speed is v₁+v₂; they meet every L/(v₁+v₂) time units, and the number of distinct meeting points is a+b (again with a:b in simplest terms).

When three or more runners are involved, pairwise meeting times can be computed, but the overall meeting of all runners at the same point occurs at the LCM of their individual round times. If runners have speeds v₁, v₂, v₃, their round times are L/v₁, L/v₂, L/v₃. The time when all meet at the starting point is LCM(L/v₁, L/v₂, L/v₃). Since L cancels, this is L × LCM(1/v₁, 1/v₂, 1/v₃) = L / HCF(v₁, v₂, v₃) provided speeds are integers. If speeds are not integers, convert to a common denominator.

A classic problem: “Two runners start together on a 400 m track. Their speeds are 5 m/s and 7 m/s. How many times will they meet in 30 minutes if they run in opposite directions?” Relative speed = 12 m/s. Time per meeting = 400/12 = 100/3 s ≈ 33.33 s. Total time = 30×60 = 1800 s. Number of meetings = floor(1800 / (100/3)) = floor(54) = 54. They meet 54 times. If the question asks for distinct meeting points, simplify speed ratio 5:7 → a=5, b=7, opposite direction → a+b = 12 distinct points.

Another twist: “A and B run on a circular track. A completes a round in 8 min, B in 12 min. They start together. After how many minutes will they meet at the starting point for the third time?” LCM of 8 and 12 is 24 min. They meet at start every 24 min. Third meeting at start = 3 × 24 = 72 min. If they run in opposite directions, the meeting at start still follows LCM of round times because both must complete integer rounds to be at the start simultaneously.

  • Assuming successive discounts add up linearly instead of multiplying the remaining fractions.
  • Using the arithmetic mean of varying interest rates for compound interest calculations.
  • Forgetting to convert profit percentage given on selling price to the equivalent on cost price.
  • Treating three‑component alligation as two independent two‑component crosses without checking consistency.
  • Taking the number of meetings on a circular track as total time divided by meeting interval without verifying distinct meeting points.
  • Applying the standard annuity formula when the first instalment is due immediately (annuity due) without the (1+R/100) factor.
  • Master these pitfalls to avoid losing marks.

hand/quantum-computing.html:
Quantum Phase Estimation and Its Role in Eigenvalue Problems

Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is the canonical subroutine for extracting the eigenphase θ of a unitary operator U when an eigenstate |ψ⟩ is available. The algorithm prepares two registers: an n‑qubit control register initialized to |0⟩⊗n and a target register holding |ψ⟩. Hadamard gates create a uniform superposition on the control register, after which controlled‑U2^k operations are applied for k = 0 … n−1. The inverse Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT†) on the control register then maps the accumulated phases into the computational basis, yielding an n‑bit approximation of θ with probability at least 4/π². The precision ε = 2−n determines the number of control qubits; achieving error ≤ ε requires O(log(1/ε)) controlled‑U powers and O(log²(1/ε)) elementary gates.

QPE underpins Shor’s factoring algorithm because order finding reduces to estimating the eigenphase of the modular‑multiplication unitary. In quantum chemistry, QPE combined with a prepared approximation to the ground state yields the ground‑state energy of a molecular Hamiltonian — this is the basis of the original quantum simulation proposal by Lloyd and later refined by Aspuru‑Guzik et al. The algorithm also appears in the HHL linear‑system solver, where phase estimation on the Hamiltonian eiAt enables controlled rotation proportional to 1/λ. A practical limitation is the need for a high‑fidelity eigenstate preparation; if the input state has overlap α with the desired eigenvector, the success probability scales as |α|². Variants such as iterative phase estimation (Kitaev) reduce the control register to a single qubit at the cost of repeated measurements, which is advantageous on near‑term devices with limited qubit count.

Error analysis shows that coherent errors in controlled‑U accumulate linearly with the number of applications, while stochastic depolarizing noise leads to an exponential decay of the off‑diagonal elements of the control register density matrix. Fault‑tolerant implementations therefore require logical controlled‑U gates with error rates below the surface‑code threshold (~10−3) and magic‑state distillation for non‑Clifford rotations appearing in U. Recent experimental demonstrations on superconducting and trapped‑ion platforms have achieved phase estimation with 3–5 control qubits, confirming the theoretical scaling but also highlighting the overhead of high‑precision controlled unitaries.

Variational Quantum Algorithms and the NISQ Paradigm

Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) treat a parameterized quantum circuit U(θ) as a trial wavefunction and optimize the parameters θ classically to minimize a cost function C(θ) = ⟨0|U†(θ) H U(θ)|0⟩ for a problem Hamiltonian H. The most prominent instances are the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for ground‑state energy estimation and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for combinatorial optimization. Both share a hybrid loop: the quantum processor prepares the state and measures expectation values (often via Pauli‑term grouping), while a classical optimizer (gradient‑free methods such as COBYLA, Nelder‑Mead, or gradient‑based methods using the parameter‑shift rule) updates θ.

Circuit depth is the primary constraint on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices. Hardware‑efficient ansätze use alternating layers of single‑qubit rotations and entangling gates native to the device topology (e.g., CNOT ladders or cross‑resonance gates). Problem‑inspired ansätze such as the unitary coupled‑cluster (UCC) operator preserve particle number and spin symmetry but require deeper circuits due to fermionic‑to‑qubit mappings (Jordan‑Wigner, Bravyi‑Kitaev). Barren plateaus — exponentially vanishing gradients with system size — have been proven for random deep circuits and certain symmetric ansätze; mitigation strategies include shallow local cost functions, layer‑wise training, and symmetry‑preserving initializations.

Measurement overhead scales with the number of Pauli terms in H. Techniques such as commuting‑group measurement, classical shadows, and derivative‑free optimization reduce the number of circuit executions. Error mitigation — zero‑noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation, and symmetry verification — improves raw expectation values without full fault tolerance. Despite these advances, rigorous convergence guarantees for VQAs remain limited; the optimization landscape is non‑convex, and the presence of local minima can trap classical optimizers. Benchmarks on 50‑qubit superconducting processors have demonstrated VQE for small molecules (H₂, LiH) and QAOA for MaxCut on 3‑regular graphs up to 20 vertices, illustrating both the promise and the current gap to practical quantum advantage.

Parameter‑Shift Rule for Gradient Estimation
Given a single‑parameter rotation gate R_x(θ) = exp(−i θ X/2) acting on a qubit, the expectation value of an observable O is f(θ) = ⟨0|R_x†(θ) O R_x(θ)|0⟩. Show how to compute the exact gradient ∂f/∂θ using only two circuit evaluations.
The parameter‑shift rule states ∂f/∂θ = ½ [f(θ + π/2) − f(θ − π/2)]. Prepare the circuit with θ shifted by +π/2, measure ⟨O⟩ to obtain f(θ + π/2). Repeat with shift −π/2 to obtain f(θ − π/2). The difference divided by two yields the exact gradient without finite‑difference error. This works because R_x(θ) is generated by the Pauli X operator whose eigenvalues are ±1, making the shift π/2 the half‑period of the sinusoidal dependence of f on θ.
Exam‑Day Strategy for VQA Questions
When a question asks about variational algorithms, first identify the ansatz type (hardware‑efficient vs. problem‑inspired) and the cost function. Remember that the parameter‑shift rule gives exact gradients for gates generated by Pauli operators; for general generators the shift equals half the eigenvalue spacing. Barren plateaus appear with deep random circuits — shallow, symmetry‑preserving ansätze are the standard mitigation. Mention measurement grouping and error mitigation as practical NISQ considerations.

Quantum Complexity Classes: BQP, QMA, and the Limits of Quantum Speedup

Bounded‑Error Quantum Polynomial time (BQP) is the class of decision problems solvable by a uniform family of quantum circuits of polynomial size with error probability ≤ 1/3. It is known that P ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE, and BQP ⊆ PP (Adleman‑DeMarrais‑Huang). The relationship between BQP and NP remains open; there is no proof that NP ⊆ BQP nor that BQP ⊆ NP. Oracle separations exist: relative to a random oracle, BQP ⊄ PH (polynomial hierarchy), while there are oracles where BQP = P. These results indicate that quantum speedup is not universal for all NP problems.

Quantum Merlin‑Arthur (QMA) is the quantum analogue of NP: a quantum verifier receives a polynomial‑size quantum witness |ψ⟩ and decides membership with bounded error. The canonical QMA‑complete problem is the k‑local Hamiltonian problem (Kitaev), which asks whether the ground‑state energy of a k‑local Hamiltonian is ≤ a or ≥ b with promise gap b−a ≥ 1/poly(n). QMA contains BQP (the verifier can ignore the witness) and is contained in PP. The class QMA(2) with two unentangled witnesses is not known to equal QMA; the separation would imply non‑trivial properties of entanglement in proofs.

Interactive proof systems with quantum provers lead to QIP = PSPACE (Jain‑Ji‑Upadhyay‑Watrous), showing that quantum interaction does not increase power beyond classical interaction. The class BQP/qpoly (BQP with quantum advice) is known to be contained in PostBQP = PP, implying that quantum advice cannot solve problems outside PP. Understanding these inclusions guides expectations: Shor’s algorithm places factoring and discrete log in BQP, but NP‑complete problems such as SAT are not known to be in BQP. The exponential speedup for unstructured search (Grover) is optimal, giving only a quadratic advantage, consistent with the BBBV lower bound. Therefore, claims of “exponential quantum speedup for all hard problems” are unfounded; the speedup is problem‑specific and tied to algebraic structure (period finding, hidden subgroups) or amplitude amplification.

Quantum Communication Protocols: Teleportation, Superdense Coding, and Quantum Key Distribution

Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown qubit state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ from Alice to Bob using a shared Bell pair |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 and two classical bits. Alice performs a Bell‑basis measurement on her qubit and her half of the entangled pair, obtaining one of four outcomes. She sends the two classical bits to Bob, who applies a corresponding Pauli correction (I, X, Z, or XZ) to his half, reconstructing |ψ⟩ exactly. The protocol consumes one ebit of entanglement and two cbits per teleported qubit; it does not violate no‑cloning because the original state is destroyed by the measurement.

Superdense coding is the dual protocol: Alice encodes two classical bits into a single qubit by applying one of four Pauli operators (I, X, Z, XZ) to her half of a shared Bell pair, then sends the qubit to Bob. Bob performs a Bell‑basis measurement on the two qubits, retrieving both bits. This achieves a channel capacity of two classical bits per qubit, double the Holevo bound for unentangled transmissions. Both protocols require high‑fidelity Bell‑pair generation and distribution; experimental implementations have achieved teleportation over 100 km of optical fiber and satellite‑based links (Micius).

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) enables information‑theoretically secure key exchange. The BB84 protocol (Bennett‑Brassard 1984) uses four non‑orthogonal states (|0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩, |−⟩) sent over a quantum channel; basis reconciliation and error correction yield a shared secret key, with security proven against general coherent attacks via the entropic uncertainty relation. The E91 protocol (Ekert 1991) uses entangled Bell pairs and tests Bell‑inequality violation to certify security device‑independently. Practical QKD systems address detector side‑channel attacks (measurement‑device‑independent QKD) and finite‑key effects. Commercial deployments exist in metropolitan fiber networks and satellite links, but distance is limited by loss; quantum repeaters based on entanglement swapping and purification are an active research area to extend range beyond the ~500 km direct‑transmission limit.

  • Confusing QPE with the Quantum Fourier Transform — QPE uses inverse QFT as a subroutine but also requires controlled‑U powers and eigenstate preparation.
  • Assuming variational algorithms guarantee global optimality — the optimization landscape is non‑convex and barren plateaus can prevent convergence.
  • Believing BQP contains NP — no proof exists; oracle separations suggest BQP and NP are incomparable.
  • Thinking teleportation transmits information faster than light — classical communication of measurement outcomes is required, preserving causality.
  • Overlooking the need for authenticated classical channels in QKD — without authentication, man‑in‑the‑middle attacks break security.
  • Equating superdense coding capacity with the Holevo bound for product states — entanglement doubles the achievable classical bits per qubit.
  • Neglecting finite‑key analysis in QKD security proofs — asymptotic key rates do not directly apply to realistic block sizes.

These advanced topics illustrate the depth of quantum computing theory that examiners expect candidates to master beyond the core algorithms and error‑correction basics.

hand/tensor-calculus.html:
Fiber Bundles, Connections, and Curvature Forms

A smooth fiber bundle π:E→M consists of a total space E, a base manifold M, a typical fiber F, and a structure group G acting smoothly on F. Local trivializations φ_U:π⁻¹(U)→U×F satisfy transition functions gUV:U∩V→G obeying the cocycle condition gUVgVWgWU=id. A principal G‑bundle is a fiber bundle with fiber G and a free right G‑action commuting with π. Associated vector bundles are constructed via a representation ρ:G→GL(V) as E=P×_ρ V.

A connection on a principal bundle is a g‑valued 1‑form ω on P satisfying ω(ξ_P)=ξ for fundamental vector fields ξ_P and R_g^*ω=Adg⁻¹ω. Its curvature Ω=dω+½[ω,ω] is a horizontal, equivariant g‑valued 2‑form. In a local section s:U→P the pull‑back A=s^*ω is the gauge potential and F=s^*Ω the field strength. For an associated vector bundle the induced covariant derivative ∇_X satisfies ∇_X(s·v)=X(s)·v+s·∇_X v and its curvature R^∇(X,Y)=∇_X∇_Y−∇_Y∇_X−∇[X,Y] coincides with the action of Ω on sections.

The Bianchi identity d_ωΩ=0 follows from dΩ+[ω,Ω]=0 and expresses the covariant constancy of curvature. In physics, the Yang–Mills action S=∫_M Tr(F∧⋆F) yields the field equations d_A⋆F=0. On a Riemannian manifold the Levi‑Civita connection is the unique torsion‑free metric connection on the frame bundle; its curvature components are the Riemann tensor R^ℓijk. The holonomy group of a connection measures the failure of parallel transport to be path‑independent and is a Lie subgroup of G determined by the curvature via the Ambrose–Singer theorem.

Characteristic Classes via Chern–Weil Theory

Chern–Weil theory assigns to each invariant polynomial P on the Lie algebra g a closed differential form P(Ω) on the base M, independent of the chosen connection. For a complex vector bundle with structure group U(n) the elementary symmetric polynomials in the eigenvalues of (i/2π)Ω give the Chern forms c_k. The total Chern class c(E)=1+c1+…+c_n lives in H2*(M;ℤ) and satisfies the Whitney sum formula c(E⊕F)=c(E)∪c(F). The first Chern class of a line bundle equals the curvature form divided by 2πi and classifies the bundle up to isomorphism.

For real bundles with structure group SO(n) the Pontryagin forms p_k are obtained from the invariant polynomials in the curvature of the Levi‑Civita connection; the Euler class e is the Pfaffian of (1/2π)Ω and integrates to the Euler characteristic χ(M) by the Gauss–Bonnet–Chern theorem. The Chern character ch(E)=Tr exp((i/2π)Ω) provides a ring homomorphism K(M)→Heven(M;ℚ) and appears in the Atiyah–Singer index formula. The Todd class Td(M)=∏i (x_i/(1−e−x_i)) where x_i are Chern roots of the tangent bundle enters the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem for complex manifolds.

Characteristic classes are topological invariants: they vanish on bundles admitting a flat connection, and they obstruct the existence of sections. For example, a non‑zero Euler class prevents a nowhere‑vanishing vector field on an even‑dimensional oriented manifold. The Stiefel–Whitney classes w_k∈H^k(M;ℤ₂) are the mod‑2 reductions of the Pontryagin classes and detect non‑orientability (w₁) and the obstruction to spin structures (w₂). The Wu formula relates Stiefel–Whitney classes to Steenrod squares, linking characteristic classes to cohomology operations.

Worked Example: Computing the First Chern Class of the Tautological Line Bundle over ℂP¹
Let L→ℂP¹ be the tautological line bundle. Using the standard Fubini–Study Kähler form ωFS normalized so that ∫ℂP¹ ωFS=1, show that c₁(L)=−[ωFS] in H²(ℂP¹;ℤ).
The curvature of the Chern connection on L is Ω = −i ωFS. The Chern–Weil representative of the first Chern class is c₁ = (i/2π) Ω = (i/2π)(−i ωFS) = (1/2π) ωFS. Since ∫ℂP¹ ωFS=1, the cohomology class of (1/2π) ωFS generates H²(ℂP¹;ℤ) ≅ ℤ. The tautological bundle has negative curvature, so its first Chern class is the negative generator: c₁(L)=−[ωFS].
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a characteristic class, first identify the structure group and the relevant invariant polynomial. Write down the Chern–Weil form explicitly, then use known normalisations (e.g. ∫ℂP¹ ωFS=1) to read off the integer class. Remember that Chern classes live in integral cohomology, while Pontryagin classes are naturally integral but often appear with a factor 2 in the de Rham representative.

Spin Structures and the Dirac Operator

A spin structure on an oriented Riemannian manifold (M,g) is a lift of the oriented orthonormal frame bundle PSO(n) to a principal Spin(n)‑bundle PSpin(n) such that the covering map Spin(n)→SO(n) intertwines the actions. The obstruction to existence is the second Stiefel–Whitney class w₂(M)∈H²(M;ℤ₂); a spin structure exists iff w₂=0. When it exists, the set of inequivalent spin structures is a torsor for H¹(M;ℤ₂).

Associated to a spin structure is the spinor bundle S=PSpin(n)×_ρ Δ_n where ρ is the spin representation of Spin(n) on the complex Clifford module Δ_n. The Levi‑Civita connection lifts uniquely to a connection on PSpin(n) and induces a covariant derivative ∇^S on S. The Dirac operator D:Γ(S)→Γ(S) is the composition of ∇^S with Clifford multiplication: D=∑_i e_i·∇e_i for a local orthonormal frame {e_i}. It is a first‑order elliptic operator, formally self‑adjoint, and satisfies the Lichnerowicz formula D²=∇^*∇+¼R where R is the scalar curvature.

On a compact spin manifold the kernel of D consists of harmonic spinors. The index of the chiral Dirac operator D⁺:Γ(S⁺)→Γ(S⁻) (when n is even) is given by the Â‑genus: ind(D⁺)=∫_M Â(M). The Â‑genus is the characteristic class associated to the power series √{x/2}/sinh(√{x/2}) evaluated on the Pontryagin forms. In dimension four, Â(M)=−(1/24)p₁(M) and the index theorem reproduces the Hirzebruch signature theorem. The existence of a non‑zero harmonic spinor forces the scalar curvature to be non‑negative somewhere, leading to the Gromov–Lawson conjecture on positive scalar curvature.

The Atiyah–Singer Index Theorem and Applications

The Atiyah–Singer index theorem states that for an elliptic pseudodifferential operator D acting between sections of vector bundles E and F over a compact manifold M, the analytical index ind(D)=dim ker D−dim coker D equals the topological index ∫_M ch(σ(D))∪Td(TM) where σ(D)∈K(T^*M) is the symbol class of D and ch, Td are the Chern character and Todd class. The proof uses K‑theory, the Thom isomorphism, and the heat‑kernel asymptotics of the associated Laplacian.

Specialising to the Dirac operator on a spin^c manifold gives ind(D⁺)=∫_M ec₁(L)/2Â(M) where L is the determinant line bundle of the spin^c structure. For the Dolbeault operator ∂̄ on a complex manifold the index is the holomorphic Euler characteristic χ(M,O)=∑(−1)^q h0,q, and the theorem reduces to the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch formula. The signature operator yields the Hirzebruch signature theorem ind(Dsign)=∫_M L(M) where L is the L‑genus built from Pontryagin classes.

Applications include the computation of the dimension of moduli spaces of instantons (via the deformation complex of the Yang–Mills equations), the proof of the positive mass theorem in general relativity using the Dirac operator on asymptotically flat spin manifolds, and the derivation of anomaly cancellation conditions in string theory where the index of a family of Dirac operators over the parameter space gives the anomaly polynomial. The families index theorem extends the result to a smooth family of operators parametrised by a base B, producing a class in K(B).

Symplectic Geometry and Geometric Quantization

A symplectic manifold (M,ω) is a smooth manifold equipped with a closed non‑degenerate 2‑form ω. Non‑degeneracy gives an isomorphism ω^♭:TM→T^*M, X↦ι_X ω. Hamiltonian vector fields X_f satisfy ιX_f ω = df; the Poisson bracket {f,g}=ω(X_f,X_g) makes C^∞(M) a Lie algebra. Darboux's theorem guarantees local coordinates (q^i,p_i) with ω=∑ dq^i∧dp_i.

A prequantum line bundle L→M is a Hermitian line bundle with a connection ∇ whose curvature is −iω. The Kostant–Souriau prequantization maps a function f to the operator Q(f)=−i∇X_f+f acting on sections of L. This representation is irreducible only after a polarization: a Lagrangian distribution P⊂TM⊗ℂ (integrable, ω|_P=0). Choosing a real polarization given by a Lagrangian foliation yields quantum states as sections covariantly constant along leaves, i.e. functions on the leaf space. A Kähler polarization (M,J,ω) with compatible complex structure J gives the holomorphic quantization where quantum states are holomorphic sections of L⊗K1/2 (the metaplectic correction).

The Bohr–Sommerfeld condition selects leaves where the holonomy of ∇ is trivial; these correspond to integral Lagrangian submanifolds. In the Kähler case the space of holomorphic sections is finite‑dimensional and its dimension is given by the Riemann–Roch formula ∫_M ec₁(L)Td(M). Geometric quantization thus links symplectic topology, representation theory of Lie groups (via coadjoint orbits), and index theory. The Guillemin–Sternberg conjecture (proved by Meinrenken and others) states that quantization commutes with reduction: the quantization of the symplectic quotient M//G equals the G‑invariant part of the quantization of M.

  • Confusing the curvature form Ω of a connection with the field strength F on the base; they differ by pull‑back via a local section.
  • Assuming every characteristic class can be represented by a polynomial in the curvature without checking invariance under the adjoint action.
  • Forgetting that the spin structure obstruction is w₂, not w₁; w₁ obstructs orientability.
  • Misapplying the Lichnerowicz formula by omitting the scalar curvature term when estimating eigenvalues of the Dirac operator.
  • Using the Chern character instead of the Â‑genus for the index of the Dirac operator on a spin manifold.
  • Neglecting the metaplectic correction in Kähler quantization, which shifts the line bundle by the square root of the canonical bundle.
  • Treating the symplectic quotient M//G as an ordinary quotient without verifying the moment map is proper and 0 is a regular value.

These advanced topics complete the bridge from abstract tensor calculus to the geometric analysis underlying modern theoretical physics and topology.

hand/quantum-field-theory.html:
Path Integral Quantization and Generating Functionals

The path integral provides an alternative to canonical quantization that makes Lorentz invariance manifest and simplifies the treatment of gauge theories. For a real scalar field the transition amplitude between field configurations φ₁(x) at time t₁ and φ₂(x) at time t₂ is written as a functional integral over all field histories weighted by eiS[φ], where S = ∫ d⁴x ℒ is the classical action. Discretising time and inserting complete sets of field eigenstates yields the formal expression ⟨φ₂,t₂|φ₁,t₁⟩ = ∫ 𝒟φ ei∫ d⁴x ℒ(φ,∂φ). The generating functional Z[J] = ∫ 𝒟φ exp{i∫ d⁴x [ℒ + Jφ]} encodes all correlation functions; functional derivatives with respect to the source J give time‑ordered Green’s functions, e.g. ⟨0|T{φ(x₁)…φ(xₙ)}|0⟩ = (−i)ⁿ δⁿZ[J]/δJ(x₁)…δJ(xₙ) |J=0. For interacting theories the functional integral is evaluated perturbatively by expanding the interaction part of the action and applying Wick’s theorem to the Gaussian free‑field measure. The same machinery extends to fermions by introducing Grassmann‑valued fields ψ, ψ̄ and to gauge fields after fixing a gauge and adding Faddeev–Popov ghost terms. The path integral also makes the derivation of Ward identities straightforward: a change of integration variables corresponding to a symmetry transformation leaves the measure invariant (up to possible anomalies) and yields relations among Green’s functions that reflect the underlying symmetry.

LSZ Reduction Formula and S‑Matrix Elements

The Lehmann–Symanzik–Zimmermann (LSZ) reduction formula connects the S‑matrix elements measured in scattering experiments to the Fourier transforms of time‑ordered correlation functions computed in the interacting theory. For an n‑particle initial state with momenta p₁,…,pₙ and an m‑particle final state with momenta q₁,…,qₘ the formula reads ⟨q₁,…,qₘ out|p₁,…,pₙ in⟩ = (i)n+m ∏i=1n ∫ d⁴x_i e-ip_i·x_i (□x_i+m²) ∏j=1m ∫ d⁴y_j eiq_j·y_j (□y_j+m²) ⟨0|T{φ(x₁)…φ(xₙ)φ(y₁)…φ(yₘ)}|0⟩. The Klein–Gordon operators (□+m²) amputate the external propagators, leaving the amputated Green’s function evaluated on‑shell. In perturbation theory the amputated Green’s function is precisely the sum of all connected, amputated Feynman diagrams with the specified external legs. The invariant amplitude ℳ is obtained by stripping the overall momentum‑conserving delta function: ⟨f|i⟩ = ⟨f|i⟩free + i (2π)⁴ δ⁴(∑p_i−∑q_j) ℳ. The LSZ formula also clarifies the role of wave‑function renormalisation: the residue of the full propagator at the physical pole defines the field‑strength renormalisation constant Z, and the LSZ reduction automatically includes the factor √Z for each external leg, ensuring that S‑matrix elements are finite and independent of the field normalisation convention.

Worked Example: Tree‑Level φ⁴ Scattering via LSZ
Compute the invariant amplitude ℳ for 2→2 scattering in a theory with interaction ℒ_int = −λ φ⁴/4! at tree level using the LSZ reduction formula.
The connected, amputated four‑point function at tree level is given by the single vertex diagram. The vertex factor from ℒ_int is −iλ. Since there are no internal propagators to amputate, the amputated Green’s function equals −iλ. Applying LSZ, each external leg contributes a factor √Z → 1 at tree level, and the overall momentum‑conserving delta function is removed. Hence ℳ = −iλ. The differential cross section in the centre‑of‑mass frame for equal masses m is dσ/dΩ = |ℳ|²/(64π² s) = λ²/(64π² s). This matches the standard textbook result.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the S‑matrix element, first write the LSZ formula symbolically, then identify the required amputated Green’s function. Remember that each external leg brings a factor of the field‑strength renormalisation constant Z1/2; at tree level Z=1, but at one loop you must include the residue of the full propagator. This step is a frequent source of missing factors in exam answers.

Renormalization Group, Beta Functions and Asymptotic Freedom

Ultraviolet divergences in loop integrals are absorbed by redefining a finite number of bare parameters. The renormalization group (RG) describes how the renormalised couplings change with the renormalisation scale μ. For a dimensionless coupling g the RG equation is μ dg/dμ = β(g), where the beta function β(g) is computed as a series in g. In quantum electrodynamics the one‑loop beta function is β(e) = e³/(12π²) > 0, so the effective electric charge grows with energy. In non‑Abelian Yang–Mills theory with gauge group SU(N) and n_f Dirac fermions in the fundamental representation the one‑loop coefficient is β₀ = (11/3)N − (2/3)n_f. For QCD (N=3, n_f=6) β₀ = 11 − 4 = 7 > 0, but the beta function is defined with a minus sign: μ dg/dμ = −β₀ g³/(16π²) + …, giving a negative β(g) and therefore asymptotic freedom — the coupling decreases at high momentum transfer. This property underlies the success of perturbative QCD in deep‑inelastic scattering and jet physics. The RG can be solved to give the running coupling α_s(μ) = 4π/(β₀ ln(μ²/Λ²)), where Λ is the dynamically generated scale. Higher‑loop corrections modify β₀ and introduce scheme dependence; the MS-bar scheme is standard for precision phenomenology. The RG also governs the scaling behaviour of composite operators through anomalous dimensions, which appear in the operator product expansion and in the evolution of parton distribution functions.

Anomalies, Ward Identities and the Axial Current

Classical symmetries that are not preserved by the regularisation of the quantum theory give rise to anomalies. The most famous is the axial (chiral) anomaly in massless QED: the classical axial current j₅^μ = ψ̄γ^μγ⁵ψ satisfies ∂_μ j₅^μ = 0, but the one‑loop triangle diagram with two vector currents and one axial current yields ∂_μ j₅^μ = (e²/16π²) εμνρσ Fμν Fρσ. This result is independent of the regularisation scheme and is exact to all orders (Adler–Bardeen theorem). The anomaly has profound physical consequences: it explains the decay π⁰ → γγ, constrains the fermion content of gauge theories (anomaly cancellation in the Standard Model), and underlies the non‑conservation of baryon number in the electroweak sector. Ward identities are the quantum counterparts of Noether’s theorem; they relate Green’s functions with an insertion of the divergence of a current to contact terms. When an anomaly is present the Ward identity acquires an extra term proportional to the anomaly coefficient. In non‑Abelian gauge theories the consistent anomaly satisfies the Wess–Zumino consistency condition, and the anomaly can be cancelled by adding a local counterterm (the Bardeen counterterm) or by arranging the fermion representations so that the total anomaly coefficient vanishes. The Standard Model achieves cancellation between quark and lepton contributions generation by generation.

Effective Field Theory, Operator Product Expansion and Power Counting

When a theory contains widely separated mass scales, the heavy degrees of freedom can be integrated out to produce an effective field theory (EFT) valid below the heavy scale. The EFT Lagrangian consists of the light‑field kinetic terms plus a tower of local operators of increasing dimension, suppressed by powers of the heavy scale Λ: ℒ_EFT = ℒ_ren + Σ_i (c_i/Λd_i−4) O_i, where d_i is the canonical dimension of operator O_i. Power counting organises calculations: at a given order in (E/Λ) only a finite number of operators contribute. The operator product expansion (OPE) provides a systematic short‑distance expansion of the product of two local operators: O_a(x) O_b(0) ∼ Σ_c Cab^c(x) O_c(0), where the Wilson coefficients Cab^c(x) encode the high‑momentum physics and are computable in perturbation theory. In deep‑inelastic scattering the OPE of two electromagnetic currents yields the twist‑two quark and gluon operators whose matrix elements are the parton distribution functions; their scale dependence is governed by the DGLAP evolution equations derived from the RG. Matching conditions at the heavy scale determine the Wilson coefficients by requiring that the EFT reproduces the full theory’s Green’s functions at that scale. Running down to low energies using the RG resums large logarithms ln(μ/Λ). This framework underlies chiral perturbation theory for low‑energy pions, heavy‑quark effective theory for B‑meson decays, and the Standard Model effective field theory (SMEFT) used to parametrise possible new physics at the TeV scale.

  • Confusing the LSZ amputation rule with the simple removal of external propagators; the correct procedure includes the Klein–Gordon operator acting on each external leg and the field‑strength factor √Z.
  • Forgetting that the beta function in non‑Abelian gauge theory carries an overall minus sign in the convention μ dg/dμ = −β₀ g³/(16π²); this sign error reverses the conclusion about asymptotic freedom.
  • Treating the axial anomaly as a regularisation artefact rather than a genuine, scheme‑independent quantum effect; the anomaly coefficient is fixed by the triangle diagram and cannot be removed by a local counterterm.
  • Neglecting the matching step when constructing an EFT; Wilson coefficients must be fixed by equating amplitudes in the full and effective theories at the heavy scale.
  • Assuming that all operators of a given dimension contribute equally; power counting and symmetries often forbid or suppress many operators, reducing the number of independent parameters.
  • Misapplying the Ward identity in the presence of an anomaly by omitting the anomaly term; the modified Ward identity is essential for deriving constraints such as the Adler–Bardeen theorem.
  • Overlooking the role of the Faddeev–Popov ghost fields in the path integral for non‑Abelian gauge theories; ghosts are required to maintain unitarity and to obtain the correct beta function.

hand/extended-tft.html:
Higher Categorical Foundations: (∞,n)-Categories and the Cobordism Hypothesis Proof Sketch

The cobordism hypothesis is a theorem about symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-categories. An (∞,n)-category has objects, 1-morphisms, …, n-morphisms, and all k-morphisms for k>n are invertible. The bordism category Bordnfr is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on a single object — the positively framed point. The proof, due to Lurie (2009) building on work of Baez–Dolan, Hopkins–Lurie, and Ayala–Francis, proceeds by constructing a presentation of Bordnfr in terms of generators and relations: the point, its dual, the evaluation and coevaluation 1-morphisms, and higher adjunction data up to level n. One then shows that any symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category C with duals admits a unique symmetric monoidal functor from this presentation sending the point to a chosen fully dualizable object X∈C. The key technical step is the “cobordism hypothesis with singularities”, which extends the classification to manifolds with stratified singularities labelled by higher morphisms in C. This yields a complete classification: the space of fully extended framed TQFTs Z: Bordnfr→C is equivalent to the maximal ∞-groupoid of fully dualizable objects in C. The framing condition can be relaxed by taking homotopy fixed points under the O(n)-action on Bordnfr, giving the oriented, spin, or unoriented versions.

Anomalies, Invertible TQFTs, and the Classification of Symmetry-Protected Topological Phases

An anomaly in a TQFT is the failure of a theory to be strictly functorial on the bordism category; mathematically it appears as a non‑trivial invertible TQFT in one higher dimension. Invertible TQFTs are those whose values on closed manifolds are invertible objects in the target category — typically complex numbers of unit modulus. The classification of invertible TQFTs in dimension n is given by the cobordism groups of manifolds with appropriate tangential structure (e.g., oriented, spin, pin±). For example, oriented 3‑manifolds have Ω3SO=0, so there are no oriented invertible 3‑dimensional TQFTs, while spin 4‑manifolds have Ω4Spin=ℤ generated by the K3 surface, yielding a ℤ‑valued invariant (the signature/16). In condensed matter, symmetry‑protected topological (SPT) phases with symmetry group G are classified by the group of invertible (n+1)-dimensional TQFTs with G‑structure, which by the cobordism hypothesis equals the homotopy groups of the Madsen–Tillmann spectrum MTG. The Freed–Hopkins theorem identifies these groups with twisted cohomology theories, giving a complete classification of fermionic and bosonic SPT phases in low dimensions. The anomaly inflow mechanism — a bulk invertible TQFT whose boundary is the anomalous theory — is precisely the statement that a non‑fully‑dualizable object in C becomes fully dualizable after coupling to an invertible (n+1)-dimensional theory.

Worked Example: Computing the Anomaly of a 2D Fermionic Theory
A 2‑dimensional fermionic theory with time‑reversal symmetry T satisfying T² = (−1)ᶠ has a potential anomaly valued in Ω3Pin⁻. Compute this cobordism group and determine whether the theory can be anomaly‑free.
The relevant bordism group is Ω3Pin⁻ = ℤ₈, generated by the mapping torus of the orientation‑reversing diffeomorphism of the Klein bottle. The anomaly of the theory is an element a∈ℤ₈. If a = 0 mod 8 the theory is anomaly‑free and can be defined on any Pin⁻ surface; otherwise it requires a 3‑dimensional bulk invertible TQFT with partition function exp(2πi a/8) on the generator. For the specific theory of a single Majorana fermion, the Arf invariant gives a = 1 mod 8, so the theory is anomalous and must live on the boundary of a 3‑dimensional invertible Pin⁻ TQFT (the “Arf invariant” TQFT).
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the anomaly group of a symmetry class, recall the low‑dimensional cobordism groups: Ω2Spin=ℤ₂ (Arf), Ω3Spin=0, Ω3Pin⁻=ℤ₈, Ω4Spin=ℤ (signature/16). Memorise the generators (K3, mapping torus of Klein bottle) and the physical interpretation (Arf invariant, time‑reversal anomaly). This turns a seemingly abstract homotopy‑theory problem into a quick lookup.

Defects, Boundaries, and the Extended Cobordism Category with Singularities

Fully extended TQFTs assign data not only to closed manifolds but also to manifolds with corners, boundaries, and codimension‑k defects labelled by k‑morphisms in the target (∞,n)-category. The cobordism category with singularities, denoted Bordnfr, sing, has objects given by (n−1)-manifolds with a stratification by defect labels, 1‑morphisms given by n‑manifolds with corners and defect networks, and so on. The cobordism hypothesis with singularities (Ayala–Francis–Tanaka, 2017) states that symmetric monoidal functors Bordnfr, sing→C are classified by fully dualizable objects equipped with a compatible system of defect data — i.e., a “singular” fully dualizable object. In practice this means that a 3‑dimensional TQFT with line defects (Wilson lines) and point defects (local operators) is determined by a modular tensor category C together with a choice of module categories over C for each boundary condition and a choice of bimodule categories for each line defect. The classification of gapped boundaries of the Turaev‑Viro TQFT, for instance, corresponds to the classification of indecomposable module categories over the input spherical fusion category. The folding trick relates a boundary condition to a domain wall between the theory and its orientation reversal, turning boundary data into defect data. This framework also captures the “holographic” relation between a 3‑dimensional TQFT and a 2‑dimensional rational conformal field theory: the latter is the boundary theory of the former, and the modular tensor category of the RCFT is the category of line operators in the bulk.

Factorization Homology and the Baez–Dolan Cobordism Hypothesis in Low Dimensions

Factorization homology (also called topological chiral homology) provides a computational tool for extended TQFTs that avoids the full (∞,n)-categorical machinery. For an n‑disk algebra A in a symmetric monoidal (∞,1)-category, the factorization homology ∫M A over a framed n‑manifold M is defined by a colimit over the Ran space of M. When A is the n‑disk algebra associated to a fully dualizable object X in an (∞,n)-category C, the factorization homology recovers the value of the corresponding extended TQFT on M. In dimension 1, an E₁‑algebra is an associative algebra; factorization homology over a circle gives the Hochschild homology, matching the 1‑dimensional TQFT value. In dimension 2, an E₂‑algebra is a braided monoidal category; factorization homology over a surface Σ reproduces the Reshetikhin‑Turaev TQFT vector space of conformal blocks. In dimension 3, an E₃‑algebra is a symmetric monoidal category; factorization homology over a 3‑manifold yields the Turaev‑Viro state sum. The Baez–Dolan cobordism hypothesis predicts that the (∞,n)-category of n‑disk algebras is equivalent to the (∞,n)-category of fully dualizable objects; factorization homology provides the explicit equivalence in low dimensions. This approach has been used to compute the TQFT invariants of mapping class groups, to prove the non‑degeneracy of the modular tensor category associated to a 3‑dimensional TQFT, and to construct the “higher genus” generalizations of the Verlinde formula.

  • Confusing the framed cobordism hypothesis with the oriented version — the framing is essential for the free generation by a point; oriented theories require O(n)-homotopy fixed points.
  • Assuming every fusion category yields a Turaev‑Viro TQFT — the Barrett–Westbury theorem requires sphericity; non‑spherical fusion categories give state sums that depend on triangulation.
  • Treating the S‑matrix of a modular tensor category as always symmetric — it is symmetric only for unitary MTCs; in general Sab = Sba holds but the matrix may not be diagonalizable over ℝ.
  • Overlooking that invertible TQFTs are classified by cobordism groups of manifolds with tangential structure, not by group cohomology alone — the Freed–Hopkins theorem identifies them with twisted generalized cohomology.
  • Misapplying the folding trick: a boundary condition for a theory T is a domain wall between T and its orientation reversal Trev, not between T and the trivial theory.
  • Believing that factorization homology works for any (∞,n)-category — it is defined for En-algebras in (∞,1)-categories, which correspond to fully dualizable objects only after passing to the (∞,n)-categorical setting.
  • Neglecting the role of the Serre functor and Nakayama automorphism in the classification of anomalous TQFTs — they appear when the target category is not pivotal, leading to a non‑trivial anomaly in the gluing axioms.

These advanced topics complete the picture of how extended topological field theories are classified, computed, and applied to topological phases of matter.
