hand/lie-theory.html:
Parabolic Subgroups, Flag Varieties, and the Bruhat Decomposition

A parabolic subgroup P of a connected reductive algebraic group G over an algebraically closed field is a closed subgroup containing a Borel subgroup B. The quotient G/P is a projective variety called a (generalised) flag variety; when P = B it is the full flag variety of complete flags in the standard representation. The Lie algebra of P is a parabolic subalgebra 𝔭 ⊂ 𝔤 containing a Borel subalgebra 𝔟. Parabolic subalgebras correspond bijectively to subsets of the set of simple roots Δ: for a subset Θ ⊆ Δ the associated standard parabolic 𝔭_Θ is generated by 𝔟 together with the negative root spaces for roots in the span of Θ. Its Levi factor 𝔩_Θ is a reductive subalgebra with root system generated by Θ, and its nilradical 𝔲_Θ is the sum of positive root spaces not in the Levi.

The Bruhat decomposition states that G = ⋃w∈W B w B, a disjoint union indexed by the Weyl group W. At the level of the flag variety this yields a cell decomposition G/B = ⋃w∈W C_w where each cell C_w = B w B / B is isomorphic to an affine space of dimension ℓ(w), the length of w. The closure relations among cells are governed by the (strong) Bruhat order on W. For a general parabolic P the relative Bruhat decomposition G = ⋃w∈W^Θ P w P uses the set W^Θ of minimal length coset representatives of W / W_Θ, where W_Θ is the parabolic subgroup of W generated by simple reflections in Θ. The corresponding cells give a stratification of G/P by Schubert varieties X_w = C_w.

Schubert varieties carry a rich geometry: they are normal, Cohen–Macaulay, and have rational singularities. Their cohomology classes [X_w] form a ℤ‑basis of the (co)homology ring H^*(G/P, ℤ). The multiplication in this ring is described by the Littlewood–Richardson rule in type A and by the generalised Schubert calculus in other types. The Borel presentation identifies H^*(G/B, ℤ) with the coinvariant algebra ℤ[𝔥^*] / (ℤ[𝔥^*]^W_+), where the ideal is generated by W‑invariant polynomials without constant term. This presentation underlies the proof of the Weyl character formula via the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem and connects representation theory to the topology of flag varieties.

Parabolic induction and restriction functors between categories of 𝔤‑modules are governed by the geometry of G/P. The Zuckerman functor Γ𝔭 (cohomological induction) produces (𝔤, K)‑modules from (𝔩, L∩K)‑modules and is central to the Langlands classification of irreducible admissible representations of real reductive groups. The Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, which compute the multiplicities of simple modules in Verma modules, also give the local intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties, linking representation theory, algebraic geometry, and combinatorics.

Cohomology of Lie Algebras and the Chevalley–Eilenberg Complex

For a finite‑dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field of characteristic zero and a 𝔤‑module M, the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex C^*(𝔤, M) computes the Lie algebra cohomology H^*(𝔤, M). As a graded vector space C^n(𝔤, M) = Hom(∧^n 𝔤, M). The differential d: C^n → Cn+1 is given by the formula (dφ)(x1,…,xn+1) = Σ_i (-1)i+1 x_i·φ(x1,…,̂x_i,…,xn+1) + Σi<j</sub> (-1)i+j φ([x_i,x_j], x1,…,̂x_i,…,̂x_j,…,xn+1). When M is the trivial module k, the cohomology H^*(𝔤, k) is a graded commutative algebra isomorphic to the cohomology of the corresponding compact Lie group (by the van Est isomorphism).

Whitehead’s lemmas state that for a semisimple 𝔤 and any finite‑dimensional module M, H1(𝔤, M) = H2(𝔤, M) = 0. Consequently every derivation of 𝔤 is inner and every central extension splits; this underlies the rigidity of semisimple Lie algebras. The Koszul complex provides a free resolution of the trivial module over the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤), yielding an alternative computation of H^*(𝔤, k) as the cohomology of the invariant subalgebra (∧^* 𝔤^*)^𝔤. By the Chevalley–Eilenberg theorem, H^*(𝔤, k) ≅ (∧^* 𝔤^*)^𝔤 as graded algebras; the primitive generators correspond to the basic invariant polynomials on 𝔤 and have odd degrees 2m_i-1 where m_i are the exponents of the Weyl group.

Relative Lie algebra cohomology H^*(𝔤, 𝔥; M) for a subalgebra 𝔥 ⊂ 𝔤 uses the subcomplex of 𝔥‑relative cochains. When 𝔥 is a Cartan subalgebra, the relative cohomology computes the cohomology of the flag variety G/B with coefficients in the sheaf associated to M. The Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence for an ideal 𝔞 ⊲ 𝔤 relates H^*(𝔤, M) to H^*(𝔤/𝔞, H^*(𝔞, M)). In the case of a parabolic subalgebra 𝔭 = 𝔩 ⊕ 𝔲, the spectral sequence collapses and yields the Bott–Borel–Weil theorem: H^q(𝔤, 𝔭; V(λ)) is non‑zero only for a single degree determined by the dot action of the Weyl group.

Continuous Lie algebra cohomology for topological Lie algebras (e.g. the Lie algebra of a p‑adic group) replaces the algebraic exterior algebra by continuous cochains. The van Est theorem identifies the continuous cohomology of a connected Lie group G with the relative Lie algebra cohomology H^*(𝔤, K; ℝ) where K is a maximal compact subgroup. This bridge is essential in the study of automorphic forms and the cohomology of locally symmetric spaces.

Worked Example: Computing H2(𝔰𝔩₂, ℂ)
Let 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩₂(ℂ) with standard basis {e, f, h} and trivial module ℂ. Compute the second Lie algebra cohomology group H²(𝔤, ℂ).
The Chevalley–Eilenberg complex for the trivial module has Cⁿ = Hom(∧ⁿ 𝔤, ℂ). Since dim 𝔤 = 3, ∧² 𝔤 is 3‑dimensional with basis e∧f, e∧h, f∧h. A 2‑cochain φ is determined by its values on these three basis elements. The differential d: C¹ → C² acts on a 1‑cochain ψ ∈ Hom(𝔤, ℂ) by (dψ)(x,y) = -ψ([x,y]) because the module action is trivial. The image of d consists of all φ such that φ(x,y) = -ψ([x,y]) for some ψ. The space of 2‑cocycles Z² = ker(d: C² → C³). Since ∧³ 𝔤 is 1‑dimensional, dφ is determined by (dφ)(e,f,h) = φ([e,f],h) - φ([e,h],f) + φ([f,h],e) = φ(h,h) - φ(2e,f) + φ(-2f,e) = 0 because φ is alternating. Hence every 2‑cochain is a cocycle: Z² = C² (dimension 3). The image B² consists of φ of the form φ(x,y) = -ψ([x,y]). The commutator subspace [𝔤,𝔤] = 𝔤 (since 𝔤 is simple), so any linear functional on 𝔤 arises as ψ∘[·,·] for some ψ. Thus B² = C² as well. Therefore H² = Z²/B² = 0. This matches Whitehead’s second lemma for semisimple Lie algebras.
Exam Strategy
When asked to compute low‑degree Lie algebra cohomology, first check whether the algebra is semisimple and the module is finite‑dimensional; Whitehead’s lemmas give immediate vanishing for H¹ and H². For non‑semisimple cases, write down the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential explicitly on a basis of ∧ⁿ𝔤; the dimensions are small enough for hand calculation in typical exam problems.

Quantum Groups and Drinfeld–Jimbo Deformations

A quantum group in the sense of Drinfeld and Jimbo is a Hopf algebra U_q(𝔤) depending on a parameter q (generic, not a root of unity) which deforms the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤) of a complex semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤. As an algebra it is generated by elements E_i, F_i, K_i±1 for each simple root α_i with relations K_i K_i-1 = 1, K_i E_j K_i-1 = qaij E_j, K_i F_j K_i-1 = q-aij F_j, [E_i, F_j] = δij (K_i - K_i-1)/(q_i - q_i-1), and the quantum Serre relations. Here (aij) is the Cartan matrix and q_i = qd_i with d_i the symmetrising integers. The coproduct is Δ(E_i) = E_i ⊗ 1 + K_i ⊗ E_i, Δ(F_i) = F_i ⊗ K_i-1 + 1 ⊗ F_i, Δ(K_i) = K_i ⊗ K_i, making U_q(𝔤) a quasitriangular Hopf algebra with universal R‑matrix satisfying the quantum Yang–Baxter equation.

When q is specialised to a complex number not a root of unity, the representation theory of U_q(𝔤) mirrors that of U(𝔤): finite‑dimensional irreducible modules are parametrised by dominant integral weights, and their characters are given by the same Weyl character formula with q-exponentials. The category of finite‑dimensional type‑1 modules is a braided tensor category; the braiding comes from the R‑matrix. At roots of unity q = eπ i / ℓ the representation theory changes dramatically: the centre enlarges, there appear non‑semisimple blocks, and the small quantum group u_q(𝔤) (a finite‑dimensional Hopf algebra) governs the modular tensor category used in topological quantum field theory and the construction of link invariants (Jones polynomial, coloured HOMFLY‑PT).

The dual Hopf algebra O_q(G) (the quantised coordinate ring) is generated by matrix coefficients of finite‑dimensional representations. It carries a Poisson–Hopf algebra structure in the classical limit q → 1, giving the standard Poisson–Lie group structure on G. The Drinfeld double construction D(U_q(𝔤)) yields a quasitriangular Hopf algebra containing both U_q(𝔤) and O_q(G) as Hopf subalgebras; its representation category is the Drinfeld centre of Rep(U_q(𝔤)). Quantum groups also arise from the FRT construction: given an R‑matrix satisfying the Yang–Baxter equation, one defines a bialgebra A(R) with generators tij and relations R T1 T2 = T2 T1 R. For the standard R‑matrix of type A this recovers O_q(SL_n).

Applications extend to integrable systems (quantum inverse scattering method), conformal field theory (the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence between representations of affine Lie algebras at critical level and quantum groups at roots of unity), and non‑commutative geometry (quantum homogeneous spaces as coideal subalgebras). The classification of finite‑dimensional irreducible representations of U_q(𝔤) for generic q follows the same highest‑weight theory as the classical case, with the crystal basis of Kashiwara providing a combinatorial model independent of q.

Affine Kac–Moody Algebras and Integrable Highest Weight Modules

An affine Kac–Moody algebra 𝔤̂ is a central extension of the loop algebra 𝔤 ⊗ ℂ[t, t-1] by a one‑dimensional centre c, together with a derivation d = t d/dt. For a finite‑dimensional simple 𝔤 with invariant form (·|·), the bracket is [x ⊗ t^m, y ⊗ t^n] = [x,y] ⊗ tm+n + m δm+n,0 (x|y) c. The Cartan subalgebra is 𝔥̂ = 𝔥 ⊕ ℂ c ⊕ ℂ d. The root system consists of real roots α + n δ (α ∈ Δ, n ∈ ℤ) and imaginary roots n δ (n ≠ 0). The Weyl group is the semidirect product of the finite Weyl group W with the coroot lattice, acting as affine reflections on 𝔥̂^*.

Integrable highest weight modules L(Λ) are those generated by a highest weight vector annihilated by all positive root spaces and on which the Chevalley generators e_i, f_i act locally nilpotently. The dominant integral weights Λ satisfy ⟨Λ, α_i^∨⟩ ∈ ℤ≥ 0 for all simple coroots including the affine one. The level k = ⟨Λ, c⟩ is a non‑negative integer. The character of L(Λ) is given by the Weyl–Kac character formula: ch L(Λ) = (Σw∈Ŵ ε(w) ew(Λ+ρ̂)) / (eρ̂ Πα>0 (1 - e-α)mult α), where ρ̂ is the affine Weyl vector and mult α are root multiplicities (1 for real roots, rank 𝔤 for imaginary roots). The denominator identity yields the Macdonald identities and, for 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩₂, the Jacobi triple product.

The Sugawara construction provides a representation of the Virasoro algebra on any integrable module of level k: L_n = (1/(2(k+h^∨))) Σm∈ℤ :J^an-m J^a_m: where J^a_m are the modes of the affine currents and h^∨ is the dual Coxeter number. The central charge is c = k dim 𝔤 / (k + h^∨). This realises the coset construction (Goddard–Kent–Olive) and underlies the classification of modular invariant partition functions in two‑dimensional conformal field theory (the ADE classification for 𝔰𝔩₂).

Vertex operator algebras (VOAs) give an algebraic framework for the chiral algebra of a CFT. The affine VOA V_k(𝔤) is generated by fields J^a(z) = Σn∈ℤ J^a_n z-n-1 with OPE J^a(z) J^b(w) ∼ k δab/(z-w)2 + fab_c J^c(w)/(z-w). Its simple quotient L_k(𝔤) is rational and C₂‑cofinite exactly when k is a positive integer (admissible levels also give rational VOAs). The representation category of L_k(𝔤) is a modular tensor category equivalent to the category of integrable highest weight modules of the corresponding quantum group at a root of unity (Kazhdan–Lusztig correspondence). This equivalence is a cornerstone of the geometric Langlands program and of topological quantum computation.

Nilpotent Orbits, the Bala–Carter Classification, and the Springer Correspondence

Let 𝔤 be a complex semisimple Lie algebra and G its adjoint group. The adjoint action of G on 𝔤 partitions the nilpotent cone 𝒩 = {x ∈ 𝔤 | ad x is nilpotent} into finitely many orbits. Each nilpotent orbit 𝒪 carries a natural symplectic structure (the Kirillov–Kostant form) and its closure ordering corresponds to the dominance order on partitions (in classical types) or to the Bala–Carter labels (in all types). The Bala–Carter theorem states that nilpotent orbits are in bijection with G‑conjugacy classes of pairs (𝔩, 𝔬) where 𝔩 is a Levi subalgebra of a parabolic subalgebra and 𝔬 is a distinguished nilpotent orbit in the derived subalgebra [𝔩, 𝔩] (i.e. an orbit meeting every simple root space of [𝔩, 𝔩]). The label is often written as a weighted Dynkin diagram where each simple root receives a weight 0, 1, or 2 according to the eigenvalues of a characteristic sl₂-triple.

The Jacobson–Morozov theorem attaches to each nilpotent element e an sl₂-triple (e, h, f) with [h,e]=2e, [h,f]=-2f, [e,f]=h. The semisimple element h defines a grading 𝔤 = ⊕j∈ℤ 𝔤_j where 𝔤_j = {x | [h,x]=j x}. The centraliser 𝔤^e is contained in ⊕j≥0 𝔤_j and its dimension equals the dimension of the orbit. The component group A(e) = Z_G(e)/Z_G(e)0 is a finite group (trivial for simply‑laced types, often ℤ/2 for non‑simply‑laced). Irreducible representations of A(e) parametrise the irreducible G-equivariant local systems on 𝒪.

The Springer correspondence is a bijection between the set of irreducible representations of the Weyl group W and the set of pairs (𝒪, ℰ) where 𝒪 is a nilpotent orbit and ℰ is an irreducible G-equivariant local system on 𝒪 (i.e. an irreducible representation of A(e)). It is constructed via the Springer resolution μ: T^*(G/B) → 𝒩, where the fibre over e is the Springer fibre ℬ_e = {gB | Ad(g-1)e ∈ 𝔫}. The top cohomology H2d(ℬ_e) (with d = dim ℬ_e) carries a natural W-action, and the decomposition of the direct image complex μ_* ℚ into intersection cohomology complexes yields the correspondence. The trivial representation of W corresponds to the regular nilpotent orbit (open dense in 𝒩) with trivial local system; the sign representation corresponds to the zero orbit with trivial local system.

Lusztig’s generalised Springer correspondence extends this to all reductive groups and to character sheaves. The geometry of nilpotent orbit closures is controlled by the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials for the affine Weyl group; the multiplicity of an irreducible representation of A(e) in the cohomology of a Springer fibre equals the value at 1 of a certain Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial. These results connect the representation theory of finite and affine Hecke algebras, the geometry of the affine Grassmannian, and the Langlands dual group.

  • Confusing the Bruhat decomposition for G/B with the relative Bruhat decomposition for G/P; the indexing set changes from the full Weyl group to minimal coset representatives.
  • Assuming Whitehead’s lemmas hold for infinite‑dimensional modules or for non‑semisimple Lie algebras; they fail in both cases.
  • Treating the quantum parameter q as a formal variable when the problem asks for specialisation at a root of unity; the representation theory changes drastically.
  • Forgetting that the level k in affine Kac–Moody algebras must be a non‑negative integer for integrable highest weight modules; negative levels give non‑integrable or non‑unitary representations.
  • Mixing up the Bala–Carter label (a Levi plus a distinguished orbit) with the weighted Dynkin diagram; the diagram is a convenient encoding but not the definition.
  • Believing the Springer correspondence matches Weyl group representations directly to nilpotent orbits; it matches them to orbit–local system pairs, and the component group can be non‑trivial.
  • Overlooking the role of the derivation d in the affine Cartan subalgebra; omitting it leads to an incomplete root system and incorrect character formulas.
The advanced sections above complete the next level of the Lie theory lesson.

hand/stochastic-proc.html:
Stochastic Filtering and the Kalman–Bucy Filter

Stochastic filtering addresses the problem of estimating the state of a partially observed dynamical system driven by noise. The classic setting: a signal process X_t satisfies a stochastic differential equation dX_t = f(X_t) dt + σ(X_t) dW_t, while observations Y_t follow dY_t = h(X_t) dt + dV_t, where W and V are independent Brownian motions. The goal is to compute the conditional distribution π_t(φ) = E[φ(X_t) | ℱ^Y_t] for test functions φ. The Kushner–Stratonovich equation gives the evolution of the unnormalized conditional density, but it is nonlinear and infinite‑dimensional. For linear Gaussian systems — f(x)=Ax, h(x)=Hx, σ constant — the conditional distribution remains Gaussian, fully described by its mean m_t and covariance P_t. The Kalman–Bucy filter provides ordinary differential equations for these moments:

dm_t = A m_t dt + P_t H^T (dY_t − H m_t dt)

dP_t = (A P_t + P_t A^T + σ σ^T − P_t H^T H P_t) dt

The first equation is a correction term proportional to the innovation dY_t − H m_t dt; the second is a Riccati differential equation for the error covariance. The filter is optimal in the minimum mean‑square sense and, under detectability and stabilizability conditions, P_t converges to a steady‑state solution of the algebraic Riccati equation. Extensions include the extended Kalman filter (linearization of nonlinear dynamics), the unscented Kalman filter (sigma‑point propagation), and particle filters (sequential Monte Carlo) for non‑Gaussian, nonlinear models. In engineering, the Kalman–Bucy filter underpins navigation, tracking, and econometric state‑space models; in finance, it appears in stochastic volatility filtering and term‑structure estimation.

Stochastic Optimal Control and the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman Equation

Stochastic optimal control seeks a control process u_t adapted to the filtration of a driving Brownian motion W_t that minimizes a cost functional J(u) = E[ ∫0^T L(t, X_t, u_t) dt + g(X_T) ] subject to the state dynamics dX_t = b(t, X_t, u_t) dt + σ(t, X_t, u_t) dW_t. The value function V(t,x) = inf_u E[ ∫_t^T L(s, X_s, u_s) ds + g(X_T) | X_t = x ] satisfies the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation, a fully nonlinear second‑order PDE:

−∂_t V(t,x) = inf_u { L(t,x,u) + b(t,x,u)·∇_x V(t,x) + ½ Tr[ σ(t,x,u) σ(t,x,u)^T ∇_x2 V(t,x) ] }

with terminal condition V(T,x)=g(x). If a smooth solution exists and a measurable selector u*(t,x) attains the infimum, then u*_t = u*(t, X_t) is an optimal feedback control (verification theorem). The HJB equation generalizes the deterministic Hamilton–Jacobi equation by the diffusion term involving the Hessian of V. In linear‑quadratic (LQ) problems — b = Ax + Bu, σ constant, L = x^T Q x + u^T R u, g = x^T G x — the value function is quadratic V(t,x)=x^T P(t) x, and P(t) solves a matrix Riccati ODE; the optimal control is linear u* = −R-1 B^T P(t) x. For infinite horizon discounted problems, the HJB becomes an elliptic PDE; viscosity solution theory (Crandall–Lions) provides existence and uniqueness without smoothness assumptions. Applications span portfolio optimization (Merton problem), consumption‑investment under stochastic volatility, queueing control, and robotics path planning under uncertainty.

Worked Example: Merton Portfolio Problem
An investor maximizes E[ ∫0^T e-ρt (c_t1-γ/(1-γ)) dt + e-ρT (X_T1-γ/(1-γ)) ] subject to wealth dynamics dX_t = (r X_t + π_t (μ−r) − c_t) dt + π_t σ dW_t, where π_t is the amount in the risky asset, c_t consumption, r risk‑free rate, μ>r, σ>0, γ>0, γ≠1. Derive the optimal consumption and portfolio rules.
The HJB equation for V(t,x)=supc,π E[…] is −V_t = supc,π { e-ρt c1-γ/(1-γ) + V_x (r x + π(μ−r) − c) + ½ Vxx π2 σ2 }. First‑order conditions: c-γ e-ρt = V_x ⇒ c = (e-ρt/V_x)1/γ. For π: V_x (μ−r) + Vxx π σ2 = 0 ⇒ π = −(μ−r)/(σ2) V_x/Vxx. Guess V(t,x)= e-ρt (x1-γ/(1-γ)) A(t)γ. Substituting yields ODE for A(t) with terminal condition A(T)=1. Solving gives A(t)= [1 − (1−e-ρ(1−γ)(T−t)/(1−γ)) (ρ−(1−γ)(r+½ θ2/γ)) / (ρ−(1−γ)r) ]-1 where θ=(μ−r)/σ. The optimal policies are c_t = x / A(t) and π_t = (θ/γσ) x. These are the celebrated Merton fractions: constant proportion in risky asset, consumption proportional to wealth.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a stochastic control question appears, first identify whether the problem is linear‑quadratic (look for quadratic cost and linear dynamics) — then the Riccati ODE is the fast track. For nonlinear problems, write down the HJB, postulate a functional form for the value function (often power or exponential), and reduce to an ODE. Always state the verification theorem conditions: V ∈ C1,2, growth bounds, and admissibility of the candidate control.

Malliavin Calculus and Integration by Parts on Wiener Space

Malliavin calculus, also called the stochastic calculus of variations, provides a differential structure on the Wiener space of Brownian paths. The derivative operator D acts on smooth cylindrical functionals F = f(W(h1),…,W(h_n)) by D_t F = Σi=1^n ∂_i f(W(h1),…,W(h_n)) h_i(t). This operator is closable from L^p(Ω) into L^p(Ω; L2[0,T]), defining the Sobolev space 𝔻1,p. Its adjoint δ (the Skorokhod integral) extends the Itô integral to non‑adapted integrands and satisfies the duality relation E[F δ(u)] = E[∫0^T D_t F u_t dt] for u in the domain of δ. The fundamental integration‑by‑parts formula E[⟨DF, u⟩L2] = E[F δ(u)] enables differentiation under the expectation sign and yields probabilistic representations of densities. A landmark result: if a random vector F = (F1,…,F_d) belongs to 𝔻1,∞ and its Malliavin covariance matrix γ_F = (⟨DF_i, DF_j⟩L2) is invertible a.s. with det(γ_F)-1 ∈ L^p for all p, then F has a smooth density with respect to Lebesgue measure. This criterion underpins Hörmander’s theorem for hypoelliptic diffusions and the regularity of solutions to stochastic differential equations. Applications include Greeks computation in finance (weight functions for Monte Carlo), sensitivity analysis of stochastic systems, and the proof of the Clark–Ocone formula: any square‑integrable ℱ_T‑measurable random variable F admits the representation F = E[F] + ∫0^T E[D_t F | ℱ_t] dW_t, which is the martingale representation theorem with an explicit integrand.

Rough Path Theory and Pathwise Solutions of SDEs

Rough path theory, developed by Lyons, provides a deterministic, pathwise framework for differential equations driven by irregular signals such as Brownian motion (Hölder exponent < ½). A rough path of order p ∈ [2,3) is a pair X = (X, 𝕏) where X_t ∈ ℝ^d and 𝕏s,t ∈ ℝd×d satisfies Chen’s relation 𝕏s,t = 𝕏s,u + 𝕏u,t + (X_u−X_s)⊗(X_t−X_u) and the p‑variation bound ‖X‖p‑var + ‖𝕏‖p/2‑var < ∞. For Brownian motion, the Lévy area 𝕏s,t = ∫_s^t (X_u−X_s) ⊗ dX_u (Itô or Stratonovich) lifts the path to a geometric rough path almost surely. The solution map Φ: X ↦ Y of the rough differential equation dY_t = V(Y_t) dX_t (V a collection of vector fields) is continuous in the p‑variation topology. This yields a pathwise solution theory without probabilistic arguments: given a realization of the noise, the solution is defined as the limit of solutions to smooth approximations, and the Itô–Stratonovich correction emerges from the choice of the area 𝕏. Rough paths also handle fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index H > ¼, stochastic partial differential equations, and provide a foundation for numerical schemes (e.g., the log‑ODE method) that preserve geometric properties. The theory has been extended to branched rough paths (Gubinelli) for non‑geometric noises and to regularity structures (Hairer) for singular SPDEs.

Large Deviations Theory for Stochastic Processes

Large deviations theory quantifies the exponential decay of probabilities of rare events for families of stochastic processes. For a family {X^ε} indexed by ε→0 (e.g., small‑noise diffusions dX^ε_t = b(X^ε_t) dt + √ε σ(X^ε_t) dW_t), a large deviation principle (LDP) holds with speed ε-1 and good rate function I(φ) if for all measurable sets A, −infφ∈A° I(φ) ≤ liminfε→0 ε log P(X^ε ∈ A) ≤ limsupε→0 ε log P(X^ε ∈ A) ≤ −infφ∈Ā I(φ). The Freidlin–Wentzell theorem gives the explicit rate function for small‑noise diffusions: I(φ) = ½ ∫0^T |φ̇_t − b(φ_t)|σ(φ_t)-12 dt if φ is absolutely continuous and φ0 = x, and I(φ)=∞ otherwise. This action functional measures the minimal “energy” required for the path to deviate from the deterministic trajectory. Varadhan’s lemma connects LDPs to asymptotics of expectations: limε→0 ε log E[exp(−F(X^ε)/ε)] = −inf_φ { F(φ) + I(φ) }. Applications include exit times from domains (mean exit time ~ exp(V/ε) where V is the quasipotential), importance sampling for rare‑event simulation, and the Wentzell–Freidlin theory of metastability in stochastic dynamical systems. The Gärtner–Ellis theorem provides an LDP for scaled cumulant generating functions, underpinning the Donsker–Varadhan theory for empirical measures of Markov processes.

  • Confusing the Kushner–Stratonovich equation (nonlinear, unnormalized density) with the Kalman–Bucy filter (linear‑Gaussian, finite‑dimensional ODEs).
  • Assuming the HJB equation always has a classical smooth solution; viscosity solutions are often required.
  • Neglecting the invertibility condition on the Malliavin covariance matrix when claiming smooth densities.
  • Treating rough path lifts as ordinary integrals; the Lévy area is essential and not determined by the path alone.
  • Misapplying the Freidlin–Wentzell rate function to processes without a small‑noise scaling or with degenerate diffusion.
  • Overlooking the verification theorem’s admissibility and growth conditions when proposing a candidate optimal control.
  • Using the Itô integral representation for non‑adapted integrands without invoking the Skorokhod integral.

Thermodynamic Foundations of Raoult’s and Henry’s Laws

Raoult’s law and Henry’s law are not empirical curiosities; they emerge directly from the equality of chemical potentials at equilibrium. For a component i in a liquid solution the chemical potential is μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln a_i, where a_i = γ_i x_i is the activity. In an ideal solution γ_i = 1, so a_i = x_i. Equating the liquid‑phase chemical potential with that of the vapour (μ_i^v = μ_iv,° + RT ln(p_i/p°)) gives p_i = x_i p_i°, which is Raoult’s law. For a solute at infinite dilution the standard state is chosen as a hypothetical 1 mol kg⁻¹ solution obeying Henry’s law; the activity becomes a2 = γ2^∞ x2 and the equilibrium condition yields p2 = K_H x2 with K_H = γ2^∞ p2°. The Henry constant therefore contains the infinite‑dilution activity coefficient and the pure‑component vapour pressure. This thermodynamic view clarifies why Raoult’s law applies to the solvent (major component) while Henry’s law governs the solute (minor component) and why both laws converge when the solution approaches ideality.

Standard‑State Choices and Their Consequences

The choice of standard state determines the numerical value of K_H. The most common convention uses a 1 mol kg⁻¹ hypothetical solution (molality basis), giving K_H in pressure units. An alternative uses a 1 mol L⁻¹ standard state (molarity basis), which introduces a density factor. In rigorous work the standard state must be stated because the van’t Hoff factor i and the activity coefficient γ are defined relative to it. For gases that react with the solvent (e.g., CO₂ in water forming H₂CO₃) the apparent Henry constant includes the hydration equilibrium; the true physical solubility constant is smaller. Textbooks often quote “Henry’s law constant” without specifying the standard state, a frequent source of confusion in competitive‑exam numerical problems.

Temperature Dependence from the Gibbs‑Helmholtz Relation

Differentiating ln K_H with respect to temperature at constant pressure yields d(ln K_H)/dT = Δ_sol H°/(RT²), where Δ_sol H° is the standard enthalpy of solution. For most gases Δ_sol H° is negative (exothermic dissolution), so K_H increases with temperature and solubility decreases — the familiar “warm soda goes flat” observation. The same relation applied to Raoult’s law gives the Clausius‑Clapeyron form for the pure‑component vapour pressure p_i°. Understanding this thermodynamic backbone allows a student to derive the temperature coefficient of any colligative expression without memorising separate formulae.

Models for Non‑Ideal Binary Mixtures

Real solutions deviate from Raoult’s law because intermolecular forces differ between like and unlike pairs. The excess Gibbs energy G^E quantifies this deviation: G^E = RT Σ x_i ln γ_i. Several semi‑empirical models express G^E as a function of composition, enabling calculation of activity coefficients γ_i and thus vapour pressures. The two‑parameter Margules equation writes G^E/RT = x1 x2 (A21 x1 + A12 x2). The parameters A12 and A21 are obtained from experimental VLE data; they capture asymmetry in the interactions. The Van Laar model, derived from a lattice‑fluid picture, gives ln γ1 = A12 / (1 + (A12 x1)/(A21 x2))² and a symmetric expression for ln γ2. Both models reduce to Raoult’s law when A12 = A21 = 0.

Wilson Equation and Local‑Composition Concept

The Wilson equation introduces the concept of local composition, recognising that the immediate neighbourhood of a molecule differs from the bulk. It writes ln γ1 = -ln(x1 + Λ12 x2) + x2 [Λ12/(x1 + Λ12 x2) - Λ21/(x2 + Λ21 x1)], with Λ_ij = (V_j/V_i) exp[-(λ_ij - λ_ii)/RT]. The volume ratios V_j/V_i and energy parameters λ_ij are temperature dependent, giving Wilson superior predictive ability for highly non‑ideal systems such as alcohol–hydrocarbon mixtures. Unlike Margules and Van Laar, Wilson cannot predict liquid‑liquid equilibrium (LLE) because it lacks a miscibility‑gap mechanism; for LLE the NRTL or UNIQUAC models are preferred.

Azeotrope Prediction and Parameter Estimation

An azeotrope occurs when the vapour and liquid compositions are equal, i.e., y_i = x_i. Using any activity‑coefficient model, the azeotropic condition reduces to γ1 p1° = γ2 p2°. For a binary system this equation can be solved for the azeotropic composition and temperature. In exam problems the parameters A12, A21 (Margules) or Λ12, Λ21 (Wilson) are often supplied, and the student must compute γ_i at the azeotropic point. A common shortcut: if the system shows a minimum‑boiling azeotrope, the total pressure curve exhibits a maximum; for a maximum‑boiling azeotrope the pressure curve shows a minimum. Recognising the curvature of the P‑x‑y diagram from the sign of G^E (positive for positive deviations, negative for negative deviations) saves time.

Worked Example: Margules Parameters from Azeotropic Data
A binary mixture of components 1 and 2 forms a minimum‑boiling azeotrope at 350 K and 1 atm. The azeotropic composition is x1 = 0.45. Pure‑component vapour pressures at 350 K are p1° = 0.80 atm and p2° = 0.60 atm. Assuming the two‑parameter Margules model, determine A12 and A21.
At the azeotrope y1 = x1 = 0.45, so γ1 p1° = γ2 p2° = P = 1 atm. Hence γ1 = 1/0.80 = 1.25 and γ2 = 1/0.60 = 1.667. For the Margules model ln γ1 = x2² [A12 + 2(A21 - A12)x1] and ln γ2 = x1² [A21 + 2(A12 - A21)x2]. With x1 = 0.45, x2 = 0.55 we have ln 1.25 = 0.2231 = 0.55² [A12 + 2(A21 - A12)·0.45] and ln 1.667 = 0.5108 = 0.45² [A21 + 2(A12 - A21)·0.55]. Solving the two linear equations in A12 and A21 gives A12 ≈ 0.73 and A21 ≈ 1.12. Both parameters are positive, consistent with positive deviation and a minimum‑boiling azeotrope.
Exam‑Day Strategy for Activity‑Coefficient Models
Memorise the functional forms of ln γ for Margules, Van Laar and Wilson. When a problem supplies an azeotropic composition and pure‑component vapour pressures, immediately write the azeotropic condition γ1 p1° = γ2 p2° = P_total. Convert to ln γ, substitute the model expressions, and solve the resulting linear system for the parameters. If only one parameter is asked, use the symmetry relation at infinite dilution: ln γ1^∞ = A12 (Margules) or ln γ1^∞ = A12 (Van Laar). This avoids unnecessary iteration.

Colligative Properties in Mixed Solvents and Electrolyte Solutions

Standard textbook derivations assume a single volatile solvent and a non‑volatile solute. In mixed‑solvent systems (e.g., water–ethanol) the vapour pressure of each solvent component follows Raoult’s law with its own mole fraction, and the total pressure is the sum. The boiling‑point elevation then depends on the combined mole fraction of all solutes relative to the total solvent moles. For a binary solvent the ebullioscopic constant K_b becomes composition dependent because the molar enthalpy of vaporisation and the molar mass of the solvent mixture change with composition. A rigorous treatment writes ΔT_b = (RT_b²/Δ_vap H_mix) x_solute, where Δ_vap H_mix is the molar enthalpy of vaporisation of the solvent mixture at its boiling point. In competitive exams this nuance appears in problems where a solute is dissolved in a known mass ratio of two solvents; the student must first compute the effective molar mass and Δ_vap H of the solvent mixture before applying the colligative formula.

Electrolyte Solutions: Debye‑Hückel Limiting Law and Extended Forms

For strong electrolytes the van’t Hoff factor i is not an integer at finite concentration because ion‑ion interactions reduce the effective number of free particles. The Debye‑Hückel limiting law gives the mean activity coefficient γ_± = 10-A z_+ z_- √I, where I = ½ Σ m_i z_i² is the ionic strength (mol kg⁻¹) and A ≈ 0.509 kg¹ᐟ² mol⁻¹ᐟ² for water at 298 K. The osmotic coefficient φ relates the measured osmotic pressure to the ideal value: π = φ i M RT. In the limit I → 0, φ → 1 and i approaches the stoichiometric ion count. At moderate concentrations the extended Debye‑Hückel equation adds a linear term B a √I in the denominator, and the Pitzer equations provide further accuracy. Exam questions often ask to estimate the degree of dissociation α of a weak electrolyte from measured ΔT_f using i = 1 + α(ν - 1), where ν is the number of ions produced on full dissociation. The student must remember that the colligative constant K_f is defined for the pure solvent, so the molality used is the formal molality of the solute before dissociation.

Association and the van’t Hoff Factor Below Unity

Carboxylic acids dimerise in non‑polar solvents such as benzene. The equilibrium 2 HA ⇌ (HA)₂ has an association constant K_a. If the total analytical molality is m, the concentration of monomer is m_m = ( -1 + √(1 + 8 K_a m) )/(4 K_a) and the dimer concentration is m_d = K_a m_m². The effective particle molality is m_m + m_d = m - m_d, giving i = 1 - m_d/m. For strong association i can approach 0.5. Problems may provide K_a and ask for the observed freezing‑point depression; the student must solve the quadratic for m_m, compute i, and then apply ΔT_f = i K_f m. A common mistake is to use the analytical molality directly in ΔT_f = K_f m, ignoring association.

Temperature Dependence of Solubility Product and the Van’t Hoff Relation

The solubility product K_sp is an equilibrium constant and therefore obeys the van’t Hoff equation: d(ln K_sp)/dT = Δ_r H°/(RT²), where Δ_r H° is the standard enthalpy change of the dissolution reaction. For most sparingly soluble salts Δ_r H° is positive (endothermic dissolution), so K_sp increases with temperature and solubility rises. However, exceptions exist: CaSO₄·2H₂O (gypsum) shows a slight decrease in solubility above 40 °C because the dissolution becomes exothermic at higher temperatures due to changes in hydration. The integrated van’t Hoff form ln(K_sp₂/K_sp₁) = -Δ_r H°/R (1/T₂ - 1/T₁) assumes Δ_r H° is constant over the temperature interval. In rigorous work Δ_r H° itself varies with temperature via the heat‑capacity change ΔC_p, leading to the Kirchhoff equation. Competitive‑exam problems typically provide K_sp at two temperatures and ask for Δ_r H° or for K_sp at a third temperature; the student must apply the integrated form correctly, using absolute temperature in kelvin.

Common‑Ion Effect Quantified with Activity Coefficients

The simple common‑ion calculation assumes ideal behaviour (γ = 1). In reality, adding a common ion increases ionic strength, lowering activity coefficients and partially offsetting the solubility suppression. The exact condition is K_sp = a_M^a a_X^b = (γ_M [M])^a (γ_X [X])^b. For a 1:1 salt, K_sp = γ_±² [M][X]. If a strong electrolyte providing the common ion is added, γ_± can be estimated from the Debye‑Hückel or Davies equation. The Davies equation log γ_± = -A z_+ z_- ( √I/(1+√I) - 0.3 I ) works up to I ≈ 0.5 mol kg⁻¹. A typical exam problem gives K_sp of AgCl, the concentration of added NaCl, and asks for the solubility of AgCl in that solution. The student must set up the mass‑balance, compute I, evaluate γ_±, and solve the resulting quadratic for the solubility. Ignoring activity coefficients leads to an underestimate of solubility by up to 30 % at 0.1 M ionic strength.

Coupled Equilibria: pH‑Dependent Solubility of Basic Anions

For salts of weak acids (e.g., CaCO₃, FeS) the anion undergoes protonation: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ ⇌ HCO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃. The overall dissolution equilibrium couples K_sp with the acid‑dissociation constants K_a1, K_a2. The conditional solubility product at a given pH is K_sp' = K_sp (1 + [H⁺]/K_a2 + [H⁺]²/(K_a1 K_a2)). This expression shows that lowering pH (increasing [H⁺]) increases the apparent solubility dramatically. Problems often provide K_sp, K_a values, and a buffer pH, asking for the molar solubility. The student must write the mass‑balance for total dissolved carbonate species, substitute the equilibrium relations, and solve for the solubility. A frequent trap is to forget the second protonation step when pH is near pK_a2.

Osmotic Pressure Method for Polymer Molar Mass Determination

Osmotic pressure π = i M RT is the most sensitive colligative property for high‑molar‑mass solutes because π remains measurable at very low concentrations where boiling‑point elevation or freezing‑point depression become vanishingly small. For a polymer solution the van’t Hoff factor i = 1 (non‑electrolyte, no association). The molar concentration M = c/M_n, where c is the mass concentration (g L⁻¹) and M_n is the number‑average molar mass. Rearranging gives π/c = RT/M_n + B c + …, where B is the second virial coefficient accounting for polymer‑solvent interactions. A plot of π/c versus c extrapolated to c → 0 yields the intercept RT/M_n, from which M_n is obtained. This is the classic “osmometric” determination of M_n. In practice, membrane osmometers operate at 25–37 °C with semipermeable membranes that retain polymer but pass solvent. The method assumes ideal dilute solution behaviour; at higher concentrations the virial expansion must be included. Exam questions may give a table of π versus c for a polymer in a good solvent and ask for M_n and the sign of B (positive for good solvents, negative for poor solvents). The student must perform a linear regression on the low‑c data, extract the intercept, and compute M_n = RT/intercept.

Light‑Scattering and Viscosity Complementarity

While osmometry gives M_n, static light scattering yields the weight‑average molar mass M_w, and intrinsic viscosity [η] provides the viscosity‑average molar mass M_v. The polydispersity index PDI = M_w/M_n characterises the breadth of the molecular‑weight distribution. For a monodisperse polymer PDI = 1; typical synthetic polymers have PDI 1.5–3.0. Competitive exams sometimes combine data: given M_n from osmometry and M_w from light scattering, compute PDI and comment on the polymerisation mechanism (step‑growth gives PDI ≈ 2, controlled radical polymerisation gives PDI ≈ 1.1). Understanding the physical basis of each average — number‑average counts molecules, weight‑average weights by mass — prevents confusion when interpreting experimental results.

Practical Considerations and Sources of Error

Membrane imperfections (pore size distribution) can allow low‑molar‑mass fractions to leak, artificially lowering the measured π and inflating M_n. Temperature fluctuations of ±0.1 K change π by ~0.3 % at room temperature, so thermostating is critical. Solvent purity matters: trace electrolytes increase π via their own osmotic contribution. The standard protocol includes a solvent blank measurement and subtraction. In numerical problems, the student may be given π values already corrected for the blank. A common error is to use the gas constant R in inappropriate units; the consistent set is R = 0.08206 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when π is in atm and c in g L⁻¹, or R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when π is in Pa and c in kg m⁻³. Unit consistency is the single most frequent cause of lost marks in osmometry calculations.

  • Assuming Raoult’s law holds for the solute at finite concentration; it is strictly valid only for the solvent in the limit x_solvent → 1.
  • Using the analytical molality directly in colligative formulas for associating or dissociating solutes without correcting with the van’t Hoff factor i.
  • Neglecting activity‑coefficient corrections in common‑ion or pH‑dependent solubility problems, especially when ionic strength exceeds 0.01 mol kg⁻¹.
  • Applying the integrated van’t Hoff equation with Δ_r H° assumed constant over a wide temperature range where heat‑capacity effects are significant.
  • Confusing number‑average, weight‑average and viscosity‑average molar masses when interpreting polymer colligative data.
  • Forgetting to convert temperature to kelvin before using the gas constant in osmotic‑pressure calculations.
  • Treating the Henry constant as temperature‑independent; it follows the same van’t Hoff relation as any equilibrium constant.

hand/birational-geometry.html:
The Cone Theorem and Extremal Ray Contractions in Higher Dimensions

The Mori cone NE(X) of a projective variety X is the closed convex cone in the real vector space N1(X) generated by classes of effective curves. The Cone Theorem (Mori, 1982) asserts that for a pair (X, Δ) with klt singularities and KX+Δ not nef, the cone decomposes as

NE(X) = NEKX+Δ ≥ 0 + Σ ℝ+[Ci],

where each extremal ray ℝ+[Ci] is generated by a rational curve Ci satisfying −(KX+Δ)·Ci ≤ dim X+1. This bound on the length of an extremal ray is sharp and is the key numerical input for the contraction theorem.

The Contraction Theorem (Kawamata, Shokurov) guarantees that for each extremal ray R there exists a morphism φR : X → Y with connected fibers such that a curve C is contracted iff its class lies in R. Three mutually exclusive types occur:

  • Divisorial contraction: the exceptional locus is a divisor; the target Y is ℚ-factorial.
  • Flipping contraction (small contraction): the exceptional locus has codimension ≥ 2; Y is not ℚ-factorial and a flip is required to continue the MMP.
  • Fano (Mori fiber space) contraction: dim Y < dim X; the generic fiber is a Fano variety with Picard number one.

In dimension three the classification of extremal contractions is explicit (Mori, 1988). In higher dimensions the structure is more subtle: the exceptional locus of a divisorial contraction can have several irreducible components, and the relative Picard number of a Fano contraction can be larger than one. The boundedness of the length of extremal rays, together with the Basepoint-Free Theorem, yields the existence of the contraction morphism in the klt setting. The Cone Theorem also underpins the proof of the Finite Generation of the canonical ring for varieties of general type (BCHM, 2010).

Log Minimal Models and the Abundance Conjecture

A log pair (X, Δ) consists of a normal variety X and an effective ℚ-divisor Δ such that KX+Δ is ℚ-Cartier. The Log Minimal Model Program (LMMP) runs the same steps as the absolute MMP but replaces KX by KX+Δ. A log minimal model of (X, Δ) is a birational model (X′, Δ′) with KX′+Δ′ nef and the discrepancies of the induced map X ⇢ X′ satisfying the usual inequalities. If KX′+Δ′ is semiample, the pair is a log canonical model.

The Abundance Conjecture predicts that for a klt pair (X, Δ) with KX+Δ nef, the divisor is semiample. It is known in the following cases:

  • Surfaces (classical, via the Enriques–Kodaira classification).
  • Threefolds (Kawamata, Miyaoka, 1992; Keel–Matsuki–McKernan, 1997).
  • Varieties with κ = 0 (Calabi–Yau type, Kawamata, 1985).
  • General type varieties of dimension ≤ 4 (Hacon–McKernan–Xu, 2014) using the ACC for log canonical thresholds.

When abundance holds, the Iitaka fibration associated to KX+Δ gives a morphism to a lower‑dimensional variety whose general fiber has Kodaira dimension zero. This fibration is the geometric incarnation of the decomposition of the birational class into building blocks: Fano, Calabi–Yau, and general type. The LMMP together with abundance therefore reduces the classification of log pairs to the study of these three types and the birational maps among them.

Worked Example: Discrepancy Computation for a Blow‑up
Let X = ℙ² and let Δ = 0. Blow up a point p ∈ ℙ² with exceptional divisor E ≅ ℙ¹. Write KY = f*KX + aE. Determine the discrepancy a and decide whether the pair (X, 0) is terminal, canonical, klt, or lc.
On ℙ² we have Kℙ² = −3H where H is the class of a line. The blow‑up f : Y → ℙ² satisfies f*H = H′ + E (where H′ is the strict transform of a line not passing through p). The canonical divisor of Y is KY = f*Kℙ² + E = −3(H′+E) + E = −3H′ − 2E. Hence the discrepancy of E is a = 1. Since a > 0, the pair (ℙ², 0) is terminal (and therefore also canonical, klt, and lc).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to classify a singularity via discrepancies, first write the canonical divisor formula for the resolution. The coefficient of each exceptional divisor is the discrepancy. Remember the hierarchy: terminal (a > 0) ⇒ canonical (a ≥ 0) ⇒ klt (a > −1) ⇒ lc (a ≥ −1). A single negative discrepancy ≤ −1 immediately rules out klt.

Termination of Flips and the Role of the ACC Conjecture

The Minimal Model Program produces a sequence of flips X0 ⇢ X1 ⇢ X2 ⇢ … . Termination means that no infinite sequence of flips exists. In dimension three Mori (1988) proved termination using the explicit classification of 3‑fold terminal singularities and the fact that each flip increases the difficulty (a certain invariant). For higher dimensions the problem remained open until Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan (2010) established termination for varieties of general type in all dimensions.

The proof hinges on the Ascending Chain Condition (ACC) for log canonical thresholds. Given a fixed dimension d and a DCC set of coefficients for Δ, the set of log canonical thresholds lct(X, Δ; D) satisfies ACC: there is no infinite strictly increasing sequence. Hacon–McKernan–Xu (2014) proved this conjecture, building on the theory of complements and the boundedness of Fano varieties. The ACC implies that the set of possible discrepancies in a bounded family is finite, which in turn forces any sequence of flips to terminate because each flip strictly increases a well‑chosen invariant (e.g., the log canonical threshold of a suitable divisor).

Termination for Calabi–Yau type pairs (κ = 0) and for Fano type pairs is still open in full generality, though recent work on the existence of good minimal models and the boundedness of complements has made substantial progress. The ACC also underlies the proof of the finite generation of the log canonical ring for klt pairs of general type.

Birational Rigidity and the Sarkisov Program

A Fano variety X with Picard number one is birationally rigid if every birational map X ⇢ X′ to another Mori fiber space is an isomorphism. Classical examples include smooth quartic threefolds (Iskovskikh–Manin, 1971) and many hypersurfaces of high degree. Rigidity means that X cannot be decomposed by the Sarkisov program into simpler pieces.

The Sarkisov program (Sarkisov, 1980; Corti, 1995) factorizes any birational map between Mori fiber spaces into a finite sequence of elementary links of four types:

  • Type I: a divisorial contraction followed by a Fano fibration.
  • Type II: a flip between two Mori fiber spaces over the same base.
  • Type III: the inverse of Type I.
  • Type IV: an isomorphism of the base varieties.

Each link corresponds to a step in the relative MMP over the base. The program reduces the study of birational maps between Mori fiber spaces to the classification of these links. In dimension three the classification of links is complete; in higher dimensions it is an active area of research. Birational rigidity is equivalent to the non‑existence of any non‑trivial Sarkisov link starting from X. Recent work (Cheltsov–Park–Shramov, 2019) uses K‑stability and alpha‑invariants to prove rigidity for many families of Fano varieties, linking birational geometry to the existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics.

Applications to Moduli Spaces and Mirror Symmetry

The boundedness of Fano varieties (Birkar, 2018) implies that for each dimension d and volume V there exists a projective scheme parametrizing ℚ‑factorial klt Fano varieties of dimension d with anticanonical volume V. This scheme can be equipped with a K‑moduli structure using the theory of K‑stability (Tian, Donaldson; Odaka, 2013; Xu, 2020). The resulting moduli spaces are proper and admit a projective coarse moduli space, providing a higher‑dimensional analogue of the Deligne–Mumford compactification of Mg.

Mirror symmetry predicts that the quantum cohomology of a Fano variety X is isomorphic to the Jacobian ring of a Landau–Ginzburg potential on a mirror partner Xˇ. The MMP provides a natural framework for constructing mirrors: a toric degeneration of X to a union of toric varieties corresponds to a sequence of flips and divisorial contractions, and the mirror potential can be read off from the combinatorics of the associated polytope. The Gross–Siebert program (2000s) uses logarithmic geometry and the MMP to construct mirror families for arbitrary Calabi–Yau varieties, while the work of Coates–Corti–Iritani–Tseng (2015) relates the quantum differential equation of a Fano variety to the Picard–Fuchs equation of its mirror. These connections illustrate how the birational classification program feeds directly into enumerative geometry and string theory.

  • Confusing the length bound −(KX+Δ)·C ≤ dim X+1 with the actual length of the extremal ray; the bound is an inequality, not an equality.
  • Assuming that every small contraction automatically admits a flip; flips exist for klt pairs (BCHM) but may fail for non‑klt pairs.
  • Treating the Abundance Conjecture as a theorem in all dimensions; it is only proved up to dimension three and for special cases in higher dimensions.
  • Misidentifying the type of a Sarkisov link; Type II links are flips over the same base, while Type I/III involve a change of the base dimension.
  • Overlooking the role of the ACC for log canonical thresholds in termination proofs; the ACC is a deep theorem, not a formal consequence of the cone theorem.
  • Believing that boundedness of Fano varieties implies finiteness of deformation types; boundedness means finitely many families, but each family may have positive‑dimensional moduli.
  • Neglecting the distinction between ℚ‑factorial and non‑ℚ‑factorial models when applying the Basepoint‑Free Theorem; the theorem requires ℚ‑factoriality of the source.

These traps highlight the subtle interplay between numerical criteria, singularity categories, and the inductive structure of the Minimal Model Program.

hand/chromatic-homotopy.html:
The Thick Subcategory Theorem and Classification of Localizing Subcategories

The thick subcategory theorem, proved by Hopkins and Smith, classifies the thick subcategories of the category of finite spectra. A thick subcategory is a full triangulated subcategory closed under retracts. The theorem states that for each integer n ≥ 0 the collection C_n of finite spectra X with K(m)_*(X) = 0 for all m < n forms a thick subcategory, and every non‑zero thick subcategory of finite spectra equals C_n for a unique n. This yields a filtration by chromatic height that mirrors the Bousfield lattice on the finite stable homotopy category.

The proof uses the nilpotence theorem to show that a map between finite spectra is nilpotent if and only if it is zero on Morava K‑theory for all heights. From this one deduces that the Bousfield class of a finite spectrum is determined by the smallest n for which K(n)_*(X) ≠ 0. Consequently the thick subcategories are linearly ordered by inclusion: C0 ⊃ C1 ⊃ C2 ⊃ … . The theorem also implies that any localizing subcategory of the whole stable homotopy category generated by a set of finite spectra is determined by the heights it detects.

An important corollary is the classification of smashing localizations on the finite category: every smashing localization is Bousfield localization with respect to a wedge of Morava K‑theories. This result underpins the chromatic fracture square and the construction of the chromatic tower. The theorem has been extended to the setting of module categories over ring spectra, where the same height filtration appears via the action of the Morava stabilizer group.

In practice, the thick subcategory theorem allows one to reduce questions about finite spectra to questions about their Morava K‑theory. For example, the existence of a v_n self‑map on a type n complex is equivalent to the non‑vanishing of K(n) on that complex. The theorem also provides a conceptual framework for the periodicity theorem: the v_n periodicity detected by K(n) is the only source of infinite families in the stable homotopy groups of spheres.

The Goerss–Hopkins–Miller Theorem and E∞ Ring Structures on Morava E-Theory

The Goerss–Hopkins–Miller theorem establishes that each Morava E‑theory spectrum E_n admits a canonical E_∞ ring structure together with a continuous action of the extended Morava stabilizer group G_n = O_n^× ⋊ Gal(𝔽p^n/𝔽_p). The theorem is proved by constructing a moduli problem for deformations of the Honda formal group of height n and showing that the resulting Lubin–Tate space carries a universal deformation equipped with an E_∞ structure. The obstruction theory for E_∞ structures is controlled by André–Quillen cohomology of the associated Hopf algebroid, which vanishes in the relevant degrees.

As a consequence, the homotopy fixed point spectrum E_nhG_n inherits an E_∞ ring structure. For n = 1 this recovers the p‑complete complex K‑theory spectrum; for n = 2 it yields a model for topological modular forms TMF at the prime p. The theorem also provides a rigid framework for the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence: the E2 term can be identified with the continuous cohomology H^*(G_n; (E_n)_*), and the E_∞ structure guarantees multiplicative compatibility with the spectral sequence differentials.

The construction uses the language of ∞‑categories and the theory of structured ring spectra. One first builds a presheaf of E_∞ ring spectra on the Lubin–Tate deformation space, then shows that the global sections compute the homotopy fixed points. The uniqueness of the E_∞ structure up to contractible choice is essential for the later development of the chromatic fracture square and for the proof of the chromatic convergence theorem.

Applications of the theorem extend to the study of the Picard group of the K(n)-local category, where the E_∞ structure on E_n allows one to compute the group of invertible K(n)-local spectra via the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence for the action of G_n on the units of E_n. This computation feeds into the classification of exotic smooth structures on spheres in high dimensions.

Worked Example: Identifying the Height of a Finite Complex
Let X be a finite spectrum such that K(0)_*(X) = 0, K(1)_*(X) ≠ 0, and K(2)_*(X) = 0. Determine the thick subcategory containing X and explain why X admits a v1 self‑map but no v2 self‑map.
Since K(0)_*(X) = 0, X is not in C0. The non‑vanishing of K(1)_*(X) shows that the smallest height detecting X is n = 1, so X ∈ C1. Because K(2)_*(X) = 0, X ∉ C2. By the thick subcategory theorem, the thick subcategory generated by X is exactly C1. The periodicity theorem asserts that a finite spectrum of type n admits a v_n self‑map; here type = 1, so X has a v1 self‑map. The vanishing of K(2) on X means X has type < 2, hence no v2 self‑map can exist.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the thick subcategory of a finite complex, first compute its Morava K‑theory at each height. The smallest n with non‑zero K(n) determines the type and the thick subcategory C_n. Remember that the thick subcategories are linearly ordered, so inclusion questions reduce to comparing these minimal heights.

The Smith–Toda Complexes and Their Role in Detecting v_n-Periodicity

The Smith–Toda complexes V(n) are finite spectra constructed inductively by killing the first n+1 generators of the stable homotopy groups of spheres at a fixed prime p. For n = 0 one takes V(0) = S0; for n = 1 the complex V(1) is the mod p Moore spectrum; higher V(n) are obtained as cofibers of v_n self‑maps on V(n-1). Each V(n) has the property that K(m)_*(V(n)) = 0 for m < n and K(n)_*(V(n)) ≠ 0, so V(n) is a type n complex in the sense of the thick subcategory theorem.

The existence of a v_n self‑map on V(n) is guaranteed by the periodicity theorem. The map v_n : Σ2(p^n-1) V(n) → V(n) induces an isomorphism on K(n) and is nilpotent on K(m) for m ≠ n. The telescope of this self‑map, denoted T(n), is a K(n)-local spectrum that plays the role of a “periodic” version of V(n). The failure of the telescope conjecture shows that T(n) does not in general agree with the Bousfield localization L_n V(n).

Smith–Toda complexes are the primary computational tool for the chromatic spectral sequence. The monochromatic layer M_n = fiber(LE(n) → LE(n-1)) evaluated on a finite spectrum X can be expressed as the K(n)-localization of X ∧ V(n). This identification allows one to compute the E1 term of the chromatic spectral sequence as π_*(M_n ∧ X) ≅ π_*(LK(n)(X ∧ V(n))). In particular, the homotopy groups of V(n) themselves provide the building blocks for the chromatic resolution of the sphere.

Recent work has extended the construction to the K(n)-local category, producing “K(n)-local Smith–Toda complexes” that detect higher chromatic information. These objects are used in the proof of the nilpotence theorem via the X(n) construction, where X(n) is a K(n)-local analogue of V(n) built from the Morava stabilizer group action on E_n.

The Chromatic Convergence Theorem and Its Proof via the Adams–Novikov Spectral Sequence

The chromatic convergence theorem states that for any finite spectrum X the canonical map X → holim_n L_n X is an equivalence, where L_n denotes Bousfield localization with respect to the wedge K(0) ∨ … ∨ K(n). This theorem asserts that the chromatic tower built from successive localizations recovers the original finite spectrum. The proof proceeds by analyzing the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) for X and showing that the chromatic filtration on the ANSS E2 term is exhaustive and complete.

The ANSS E2 term is ExtBP_*BPs,t(BP_*, BP_*X). The chromatic filtration on this Ext group is induced by the filtration of the Hopf algebroid (BP_*, BP_*BP) by the ideals I_n = (p, v1, …, vn-1). The associated graded pieces are the cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group with coefficients in (E_n)_*X, which compute the homotopy groups of the monochromatic layers M_n ∧ X. The convergence of the ANSS for finite spectra, together with the vanishing line of slope 1/(p-1), implies that the inverse limit of the localizations L_n X recovers X.

A key technical ingredient is the nilpotence theorem, which guarantees that any map between finite spectra that is zero on all Morava K‑theories is nilpotent. This allows one to replace the Bousfield localization L_n by the smashing localization with respect to the telescope T(n) on the finite category, up to phantom maps. The chromatic convergence theorem then follows from the fact that the tower of telescopes T(n) is pro‑equivalent to the tower of localizations L_n on finite spectra.

The theorem has profound consequences: it justifies the chromatic approach to computing stable homotopy groups of spheres, because any finite spectrum can be reconstructed from its K(n)-localizations. It also underlies the chromatic fracture square, which expresses LK(n)X as a homotopy pullback of LE(n)X and LE(n-1)X. In the K(n)-local category, the convergence theorem implies that the category is generated by the single compact object K(n), making it a compactly generated triangulated category.

The Gross–Hopkins Duality and Its Consequences for Duality in the K(n)-Local Category

Gross–Hopkins duality provides a canonical equivalence between the Spanier–Whitehead dual of the Morava E‑theory spectrum E_n and a suspension of E_n itself. Precisely, there is an equivalence I_n ≃ Σn2-n E_n^∨, where I_n denotes the Gross–Hopkins dual of the K(n)-local sphere. The duality is constructed using the action of the Morava stabilizer group G_n on E_n and the fact that the determinant character of G_n gives a one‑dimensional representation whose associated invertible K(n)-local spectrum is the dualizing object.

The duality formula for Morava K‑theory states that the Brown–Comenetz dual of K(n) is Σ2(p^n-1)n K(n). This follows from the identification of the Gross–Hopkins dual with the Anderson dual in the K(n)-local category and the computation of the Picard group. The shift exponent n2-n reflects the dimension of the formal group and the degree of the determinant character.

Consequences of Gross–Hopkins duality include a Poincaré duality for the K(n)-local category: for any K(n)-local spectrum X there is a natural equivalence between the mapping spectrum FK(n)(X, I_n) and the suspension Σ-n2+n X. This duality is used to compute the homotopy groups of the K(n)-local sphere via the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence for the action of G_n on E_n, because the dualizing object I_n is the cohomological dual of the sphere.

In the context of the chromatic spectral sequence, Gross–Hopkins duality implies a symmetry of the E1 term: the monochromatic layers satisfy M_n ≃ Σn2-n M_n^∨. This symmetry is reflected in the pattern of differentials in the chromatic spectral sequence and provides constraints on possible exotic extensions in the stable homotopy groups of spheres. The duality also plays a central role in the proof of the nilpotence theorem via the X(n) construction, where the self‑duality of X(n) is essential for the induction on height.

  • Confusing the thick subcategory C_n with the localizing subcategory generated by K(n); they coincide on finite spectra but differ on infinite spectra.
  • Assuming the telescope T(n) is always equivalent to the localization L_n on all spectra; the telescope conjecture fails in general.
  • Neglecting the shift in Gross–Hopkins duality; the suspension degree n2-n is crucial for correct duality statements.
  • Treating the Goerss–Hopkins–Miller theorem as providing a unique E_∞ structure without mentioning the contractible space of choices.
  • Overlooking the role of the nilpotence theorem in the proof of chromatic convergence; it is the bridge between algebraic detection and geometric reconstruction.
  • Misidentifying the type of a Smith–Toda complex by checking only K(n) and forgetting that K(m) for m < n must vanish.
  • Forgetting that the chromatic convergence theorem applies only to finite spectra; infinite spectra need not be recovered by the tower.

These advanced topics complete the core theoretical toolkit required for research-level work in chromatic homotopy theory.

hand/scattering-theory.html:
Multichannel Scattering and the Analytic Structure of the S‑Matrix

In realistic quantum systems several asymptotic channels are open simultaneously. The Hilbert space splits as a direct sum H = ⊕α Hα where each channel α carries a free Hamiltonian H0,α. The full Hamiltonian H = H0 + V couples the channels through off‑diagonal potentials Vαβ. The Møller operators Ω± become block matrices Ω±,αβ mapping incoming channel β to outgoing channel α. Their strong limits exist under the usual short‑range condition ∫ (1+|x|) |V(x)| dx < ∞ for each matrix element.

The multichannel S‑matrix S(λ) = Ω+* Ω− is a unitary matrix‑valued function on the continuous spectrum. Its diagonal blocks Sαα(λ) describe elastic scattering within a channel, while off‑diagonal blocks Sαβ(λ) (α ≠ β) encode inelastic transition amplitudes. Unitarity S(λ) S(λ)* = I yields the optical theorem for each channel: Im fαα(θ=0) = (kα/4π) σα,tot, where σα,tot = Σβ ∫ |Sαβ(θ)|² dΩ.

Analytic continuation of S(λ) into the complex energy plane reveals a rich pole structure. Besides bound‑state poles on the negative real axis (physical sheet) and resonance poles on the second sheet, multichannel systems exhibit branch points at each channel threshold λ = Ethr,α. Near a threshold the S‑matrix behaves as Sαβ(λ) ∼ Cαβ (λ−Ethr,α)ℓ+½ where ℓ is the orbital angular momentum of the incoming partial wave. This threshold law (Wigner’s law) governs low‑energy cross sections and is crucial for cold‑atom physics.

The Jost matrix J(k) provides a factorisation S(k) = J(−k) J(k)−1 for each channel momentum k. Its determinant is the Jost function; zeros of det J(k) in the upper half‑plane correspond to bound states, while zeros in the lower half‑plane on the unphysical sheet correspond to resonances. The multichannel Jost matrix is analytic in a cut plane and satisfies the symmetry J(−k) = J(k)† for real k, guaranteeing unitarity of S(k).

Applications include nuclear reaction theory (R‑matrix formalism), electron‑molecule scattering (close‑coupling equations), and ultracold collisions where magnetic Feshbach resonances are described by a two‑channel model with a closed‑channel bound state crossing the open‑channel threshold. The analytic structure of the multichannel S‑matrix thus unifies bound states, resonances, and threshold phenomena in a single framework.

Trace Formulas, the Krein Spectral Shift, and the Birman–Krein Identity

The spectral shift function ξ(λ; H, H₀) measures the net change in the density of states caused by the perturbation V = H − H₀. For trace‑class perturbations the Krein trace formula holds: Tr [f(H) − f(H₀)] = ∫ℝ f′(λ) ξ(λ) dλ for every f ∈ C1(ℝ) with f′ ∈ L¹(ℝ). This identity extends the classical Lifshits–Krein formula to a wide class of functions, including the resolvent f(z) = (z−λ)−1 which yields the Krein spectral shift representation of the perturbation determinant D(z) = det(I + V R₀(z)).

The Birman–Krein formula connects the scattering matrix to the spectral shift: det S(λ) = e−2πi ξ(λ) for a.e. λ ∈ σc(H₀). Taking the logarithmic derivative gives the celebrated relation ξ(λ) = (1/2πi) Tr[ S(λ)* S′(λ) ], which expresses the spectral shift as the winding number of the S‑matrix eigenvalues on the unit circle. This formula is the cornerstone of the topological interpretation of Levinson’s theorem in multichannel scattering: the total phase shift accumulated across all open channels equals π times the number of bound states plus contributions from half‑bound states at thresholds.

For non‑trace‑class but relatively trace‑class perturbations (e.g. short‑range potentials in dimension d ≥ 3) the spectral shift function still exists as an L¹ function and the trace formula holds for f with sufficient decay. The proof uses the limiting absorption principle for the resolvent and the fact that the difference of the spectral measures is absolutely continuous with density ξ(λ). The Birman–Krein identity then follows from the stationary representation of the wave operators and the intertwining property S(λ) = I − 2πi T(λ) where T(λ) is the on‑shell T‑matrix.

Applications of the trace formula are manifold. In random matrix theory the spectral shift function of a rank‑one perturbation yields the celebrated “determinantal” formula for the eigenvalue distribution. In quantum chaos the Gutzwiller trace formula can be derived as a semiclassical approximation to the Krein trace formula for the scattering matrix of a chaotic cavity. In mathematical physics the spectral shift function appears in the definition of the η‑invariant and the spectral flow, linking scattering theory to index theory on manifolds with boundary.

Worked Example: Birman–Krein for a Rank‑One Perturbation
Let H₀ = −Δ on L²(ℝ³) and V = −α |φ⟩⟨φ| with φ ∈ L², ‖φ‖ = 1, α > 0. Compute the spectral shift function ξ(λ) and verify det S(λ) = e−2πi ξ(λ).
The perturbation determinant is D(z) = 1 − α ⟨φ, R₀(z) φ⟩. For Im z > 0, ⟨φ, R₀(z) φ⟩ = ∫ |φ̂(k)|²/(k²−z) d³k. Its boundary value on the positive real axis λ = k² gives ⟨φ, R₀(λ+i0) φ⟩ = P∫ |φ̂(k)|²/(k²−λ) d³k − iπ ∫|k|=√λ |φ̂(k)|² dΩ. Hence Im log D(λ+i0) = −arctan( απ ρ(λ) / (1−α P∫…) ) where ρ(λ) = ∫|k|=√λ |φ̂(k)|² dΩ. The spectral shift is ξ(λ) = (1/π) Im log D(λ+i0). The on‑shell T‑matrix is T(λ) = −α |φ⟩⟨φ| / D(λ+i0). The S‑matrix is S(λ) = I − 2πi T(λ) δ(H₀−λ). Its determinant on the continuous spectrum reduces to det S(λ) = 1 − 2πi Tr[T(λ) δ(H₀−λ)] = 1 − 2πi (−α ρ(λ)/D) = D(λ−i0)/D(λ+i0) = e−2πi ξ(λ). The identity holds.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the spectral shift function of a rank‑one or finite‑rank perturbation, write down the perturbation determinant D(z) = det(I + V R₀(z)) immediately. The spectral shift is ξ(λ) = (1/π) limε→0⁺ Im log D(λ+iε). The Birman–Krein formula then gives det S(λ) = D(λ−i0)/D(λ+i0). This shortcut avoids computing the full S‑matrix and is a favourite in advanced problem papers.

Scattering on Non‑Compact Manifolds and the Lax–Phillips Semigroup

The Lax–Phillips framework was originally devised for the wave equation on the exterior of a compact obstacle in ℝⁿ. It extends naturally to complete Riemannian manifolds (M,g) with a compact trapped set and an infinite cylindrical end. The Hilbert space is H = L²(M) ⊕ L²(M) for the first‑order system (u, ∂tu). The free dynamics U₀(t) is the wave group on the cylindrical end (a translation representation), while the interacting dynamics U(t) is the wave group on M. The incoming and outgoing subspaces D−, D+ are defined as the orthogonal complements of the subspaces of solutions that vanish on the cylindrical end for t ≤ 0 and t ≥ 0 respectively.

The Lax–Phillips semigroup Z(t) = P+ U(t) P− acts on the “outgoing translation representation” K = D− ⊖ U(−t) D− for t > 0. Its generator B has spectrum contained in the left half‑plane; the eigenvalues of B are precisely the resonances of the obstacle (or of the manifold). The semigroup is completely non‑unitary and contractive: ‖Z(t)‖ ≤ e−γ t where γ is the distance from the imaginary axis to the nearest resonance. This exponential decay of local energy is the hallmark of non‑trapping geometries; for trapping obstacles the decay is only polynomial and the semigroup has a non‑trivial Jordan block at the origin.

The translation representation identifies K with L²(ℝ₊; ℋ) where ℋ is the space of Cauchy data on a cross‑section of the cylindrical end. In this representation Z(t) is simply the right‑shift (Z(t)f)(s) = f(s+t). The scattering matrix S(λ) becomes a unitary operator on ℋ for each frequency λ, and the Lax–Phillips theory proves that S(λ) extends meromorphically to the complex plane with poles exactly at the resonances. The Poisson formula for the wave trace reads Tr[U(t) − U₀(t)] = Σresonances ρ e−iρ t + smooth terms, linking the geometry of the trapped set to the distribution of resonances.

Important developments include the Mazzeo–Melrose theory for asymptotically hyperbolic manifolds, where the conformal compactification turns the resolvent into a meromorphic family of operators on weighted Sobolev spaces. The Selberg zeta function on hyperbolic surfaces appears as the Fredholm determinant of the scattering matrix, and its zeros are the resonances of the Laplacian. The Lax–Phillips semigroup also underlies the proof of the fractal Weyl law for open quantum chaotic systems: the number of resonances in a strip |Im ρ| ≤ C grows like h−δ where δ is the fractal dimension of the trapped set.

Inverse Scattering Transform for Integrable Nonlinear Equations

The inverse scattering transform (IST) solves certain nonlinear evolution equations by linearising them through a Lax pair. For the Korteweg–de Vries equation ut − 6 u ux + uxxx = 0 the Lax pair is L = −∂x² + u(x,t), ∂tL = [L, A] with A = −4∂x³ + 6 u ∂x + 3 ux. The spectrum of L is invariant under the flow; the continuous spectrum is [0,∞) and the discrete eigenvalues −κj² correspond to solitons. The scattering data consist of the reflection coefficient r(k,t), the bound‑state norms cj(t), and the eigenvalues κj. Their time evolution is trivial: r(k,t) = r(k,0) e8 i k³ t, cj(t) = cj(0) e8 κj³ t.

Reconstruction of u(x,t) from the scattering data uses the Gel'fand–Levitan–Marchenko integral equation. For the reflectionless case (r ≡ 0) the solution is an N‑soliton: u(x,t) = −2 ∂x² log det(I + C(x,t)) where Cij = ci cj e−(κi+κj)x + 8(κi³+κj³)t / (κi+κj). The general solution with non‑zero reflection coefficient is obtained by solving the Marchenko equation K(x,y) + F(x+y) + ∫x∞ K(x,s) F(s+y) ds = 0, where F(z) = (1/2π) ∫ r(k) ei k z dk + Σ cj e−κj z. Then u(x,t) = −2 ∂x K(x,x).

The IST extends to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation i ψt + ψxx + 2|ψ|² ψ = 0 (Zakharov–Shabat system), the sine‑Gordon equation, and the Kadomtsev–Petviashvili equation. In each case the direct scattering problem is a linear spectral problem (Schrödinger, Dirac, or non‑local) and the inverse problem is a Riemann–Hilbert factorisation on the complex spectral plane. The long‑time asymptotics of solutions are obtained by the Deift–Zhou steepest‑descent method for oscillatory Riemann–Hilbert problems, yielding soliton resolution conjectures for a wide class of integrable PDEs.

Recent advances include the IST for non‑local integrable equations (e.g. the non‑local NLS with PT‑symmetry), the inverse scattering for the focusing NLS with nonzero boundary conditions (modulational instability), and the use of the dressing method to generate multi‑soliton solutions on non‑zero backgrounds. These techniques have found applications in fibre optics, water‑wave modelling, and the study of rogue waves.

Numerical Computation of Resonances via Complex Scaling and Perfectly Matched Layers

Resonances are eigenvalues of the non‑self‑adjoint operator obtained after complex scaling (dilation analyticity). For a dilation‑analytic potential V(x) the family H(θ) = e−2iθ (−Δ) + V(eiθ x) is analytic in θ ∈ [0, θ₀). Its discrete eigenvalues in the sector −2θ < arg z < 0 are independent of θ and coincide with the physical resonances. The method reduces the computation to a standard eigenvalue problem for a non‑Hermitian matrix after discretisation (finite elements, spectral methods). The eigenvalues converge exponentially with the basis size for analytic potentials.

Perfectly matched layers (PML) provide an alternative that works for non‑analytic potentials and on general domains. One surrounds the computational domain with a layer where the coordinates are stretched by a complex factor s(x) = 1 + i σ(x)/ω. The Helmholtz equation (Δ + k² n²) u = 0 becomes ∇·(S⁻¹ ∇u) + k² n² det S u = 0 with S = diag(s₁, s₂, s₃). The PML parameters σ(x) are chosen to increase smoothly from zero at the interface to a maximum at the outer boundary, minimising spurious reflections. The resulting non‑Hermitian eigenvalue problem yields approximations to resonances; the error decays exponentially with the PML thickness and the polynomial order of σ.

Both methods produce a discrete set of complex eigenvalues. Physical resonances are identified by their stability under variation of the scaling angle θ or the PML parameters, while numerical artifacts (PML modes) move with the parameters. The computed resonances can be used to construct the scattering matrix via the pole expansion S(λ) ≈ I + Σj (Rj)/(λ−λj) where Rj are rank‑one residues obtained from the resonant states. This pole representation is the basis of the “resonance expansion” of the time‑dependent wave field and of the design of metamaterials with tailored resonance spectra.

State‑of‑the‑art software packages (e.g. RESONANCES, MPB, COMSOL) implement complex scaling and PML with high‑order finite elements and adaptive mesh refinement. Benchmark problems include the hydrogen atom in a strong field (Stark resonances), dielectric microcavities (whispering‑gallery modes), and quantum dots with open boundaries. The convergence theory relies on the analytic Fredholm theorem for the complex‑scaled resolvent and on the exponential convergence of PML for non‑trapping geometries.

  • Confusing the multichannel S‑matrix with the single‑channel S‑matrix and forgetting the threshold branch points.
  • Assuming the Birman–Krein formula holds for all perturbations without checking the trace‑class or relatively trace‑class condition.
  • Misidentifying the Lax–Phillips semigroup generator spectrum with the full Hamiltonian spectrum instead of the resonance set.
  • Neglecting the time evolution of the reflection coefficient in the IST and treating it as static.
  • Treating PML eigenvalues as physical resonances without verifying parameter stability.
  • Overlooking the Wigner threshold law when analysing low‑energy cross sections in multichannel problems.
  • Applying the Krein trace formula to functions f that are not sufficiently regular, leading to divergent integrals.
